Translator's Preface
b
When I first placed my hands on these three books, I did not
know I would come away from them carrying more than I had
brought to them. I began the work as someone tasked with
carrying meaning from one language into another, only to find
myself a student before an integrated intellectual project: one
that reorders the Muslim's relationship with the self, with the
stations of faith, and with religion in the full breadth of its
civilizational reach.
Knowing the Self: The Path to Uprightness, The Balance of
b
Spiritual Stations in the Muslim's Life, and Reviving
b
Religion in the Self and Life,
b
three titles, yet at their core a
single, continuous journey: from the self to the station, and
from the station to life in its entirety. In carrying these books
into English, I have taken care to remain faithful to this
sequence, rendering a connected argument rather than
sentences cut loose from their context.
The greatest responsibility I felt as I translated was preserving
the precise interweaving, so characteristic of these books,
between the sacred text, whether a Qur'anic verse, a hadith, or
a scholar's statement, and the educational commentary that so
often follows it. This double register is not padding; it is the
very heart of the method the author chose to bring sacred
meaning within reach of the non-specialist reader without
compromising its precision. I have rendered the meanings of
the verses and hadiths through my own careful effort, out of
scholarly conscientiousness, rather than borrowing a ready-
made translation that might not sit naturally within the
commentary surrounding it in the original.
The greater challenge, though, was never simply carrying a
word across, but rather carrying a spirit. How does one
translate a term like
Istiqamah
b
(uprightness),
'ubudiyyah
b
(servitude), or
Istislam
b
(submission) into English without its
weight being lost, without it collapsing into a pale synonym
that carries only the husk of the meaning and none of its
substance? At every turn I had to weigh terminological
precision against clarity for a reader who may not carry a deep
grounding in the religious sciences.
I hope this translation has done some justice to these books
before their new readers, and that it opens a door for them
toward a wide readership that yearns, as so many of my own
generation yearn, for an understanding of religion that unites
fidelity to the text with the vitality of its living application.
I ask Allah to make this effort sincerely for His sake, and of
benefit both to the author of these books and to every reader
who encounters them in a language other than their own.
Sidy Ahmad Gassama

Introduction to the Book
b
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
i
All praise is due to Allah, who sent down religion as guidance
for the human being, not a burden upon him, and made it a
path for life, not rites cut off from reality. I bear witness that
there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and I bear
witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, who
conveyed the message, established the balance, and left us
upon the clear, radiant way.
To proceed: the greatest affliction to have befallen this nation
(ummah) in our time is not the onslaught of enemies, nor the
acceleration of technology, nor the changing world, it is the
misunderstanding of this religion: either a rigid understanding
that has reduced it to lifeless moulds, or a hollowed-out
understanding that has stripped it of its spirit and its purposes.
The world has entered a new phase, in which concepts have
shifted, minds have grown entangled, and culture, politics,
economics, and technology have become interwoven. The
human being now lives within a single global network, amid
accelerating pressures, great questions, and a mounting
existential unease. During this scene, a fundamental question
arises: is Islam fit for this world? Or has the world moved
beyond it?
This question (however innocent it may appear to some) is, in
truth, the product of ignorance of the true nature of this
religion, for Islam has never been a mere reaction to reality; it
has always been a shaper of reality, an architect of civilization,
and a guide of humanity. Hence this book,
The Balanced Scale:
i
A Contemporary Reading of Islam
i
, is a sincere attempt to present
Islam not as a heritage to be merely preserved, nor slogans to
be raised, but as a comprehensive system for living that
understands the human being, builds the mind, purifies the
spirit, and orders society.
This book does not address specialists alone, nor does it
content itself with bare exhortation; rather, it seeks to simplify
the great concepts, and to connect the pillars of faith and the
acts of worship to their purposes, their effects, and their
function in building the contemporary human being.
It is a candid call to move from a religion of habit to a religion
of awareness, from formal commitment to civilizational
commitment, and from an isolated, individualistic Islam to an
Islam active in the world.
If I am right, it is from Allah alone; and if I have erred, and no
doubt I have, it is from myself and from Satan, and Allah and
His Messenger are innocent of it.
Our final call is that all praise is due to Allah, Lord of all the
worlds.

the question of our age is no longer,
“Do we believe?” but rather the deeper question has become:
“How do we understand what we believe?”
For many of the crises afflicting the Muslim today do not go
back to any weakness in the text, nor to any lack of guidance,
but rather to a defect in understanding, or to a disturbance in
applying religion to a changing reality, or to a flaw in the path
of understanding religion, in the manner of receiving
knowledge, and in the method of its application. How much
truth has been misunderstood until it turned into falsehood;
and how much guidance has been confined within rigid
moulds until it became a burden rather than a mercy.
The world today lives through unprecedented
transformations: an acceleration of knowledge, an explosion
of technology, an intellectual fluidity, and an unprecedented
intermingling of cultures and identities. During this scene,
many Muslims find themselves at a crossroads: either a retreat
into a traditional understanding that does not answer the
questions of the age, or a dissolving into a new reality that
empties religion of its essence.
From this arises the pressing need to reopen the file of
understanding religion, not to rewrite the texts, nor to revisit
its fixed principles, but to reconnect religion with its original
function: guiding the human being and building life according
to time and place.
This Part is not a defence of Islam, for Islam has no need of
defence; it is, rather, an attempt to reorder our angle of vision,
so that religion may be understood as Allah intended it:
guidance, construction, and a balance for life.
Islam is an eternal message, valid for every time and place,
capable of addressing the human being at every stage of life,
however much his tools and his questions may change. This

Chapter 1: Why Do We Need Today to Re-Understand
b
Religion?
b
Not because religion is deficient, nor because revelation falls
short, but because the human being has changed, reality has
shifted, and the questions have grown more complex, so an
understanding that arose within a particular historical context
may not, on its own, be sufficient to answer the challenges of
a new context, even though the text remains one and the truth
remains fixed.
The first Muslims did not ask whether this religion was fit for
life, because they saw it building life before their very eyes; but
the difficulty arose when religion moved, in people’s minds,
from being the leader of reality to being reality’s follower.
The need to re-understand religion never means reinventing
religion, nor casting doubt upon its fixed principles, nor
reinterpreting it according to the whims of the age, it means
one single, grave and important thing: liberating
understanding from the moulds in which it has been frozen,
or which have been emptied of meaning.
The world has changed; patterns of thought have changed; the
nature of the questions has changed; the means of influence
have changed; and the human being’s image of himself and of
the cosmos has changed, while religious discourse, in many
instances, has continued to repeat the same answers, without
ever touching the new questions, or consciously connecting
the text to reality. Thus, a generation arose that knows the
rulings but does not grasp their wisdom, that performs the acts
of worship but does not feel their effects, that belongs to
religion yet feels estranged from it in the details of daily life.
Hence re-understanding became a religious and civilizational
necessity, not an intellectual luxury.
The contemporary human being has moved from a world of
simplicity to a world of complexity, from local life to global
life, from a slow rhythm to a feverish acceleration, and in the
face of this transformation, it is no longer enough to be content
with reductive answers or emotional discourse. Rather, the
Muslim has come to need a conscious, balanced
understanding, one that unites text and purpose, the fixed and
the variable.
Re-understanding does not mean renewing religion itself, but
renewing our understanding of religion, that is, moving from
rote instruction to awareness, from repetition to
comprehension, and from an unexamined inheritance to an
insightful understanding.
Chapter 2: The Difference Between the Fixed Principles of
b
Religion and the Variables of Reality
b
Among the greatest confusions that have troubled
contemporary Islamic thought is the conflation of what is
fixed in religion, and does not change, with what is variable in
reality, and shifts with the changing of time, place, and
circumstance.
The fixed principles of religion are the great fundamentals that
do not change with the changing of time and circumstance:
1. Creed, in all its requirements, that is: faith, monotheism,
revelation, moral values, and the fixed general purposes,
these do not change.
2. The Shari’ah, in all its requirements, that is, the acts of
worship made obligatory by definitive texts. These are
not subject to negotiation, nor do they admit substitution,
for they are bound up with the very reality of religion and
with the human being’s own innate disposition (fitrah).
As for the variables, they are the means of application, the
methods of calling people to Islam, the forms of organization,
and the human efforts of independent reasoning (ijtihad) that
are governed by benefit, circumstance, and reality. These
change with the changing of time, place, or circumstance, vary
with varying conditions, and diversify in their means and
patterns, and herein lies the wonder of Islam and its capacity
to engage with every age without losing its identity.
Freezing the variables in the name of preserving religion
produces rigidity, just as dissolving the fixed principles, that
is, altering, diluting, or distorting religious fundamentals, in
the name of keeping pace with the age produces deviation.
The precise balance lies in combining fixity of reference with
flexibility of application. The gravest disorder occurs when we
turn the variable into religion itself or subject the fixed to the
whims of reality: some people have frozen religion in
historical forms, as though Islam had descended to live in a
single age alone; others have dissolved religion into reality,
until nothing of it remains but the name.
The correct method is fixity in fundamentals, flexibility in
means, awareness of purposes, and a sound grasp of reality.
For the Shari’ah did not come to clash with innate human
nature, nor to break the movement of life, but came to direct
it, purify it, and prevent its deviation.
Chapter 3: Religion Between Rigidity and Unrestraint
b
Religion has, in many ages, been afflicted by two opposite
extremes: a rigidity that reduces religion to appearances and
forms and turns it into rituals devoid of spirit; and an
unrestraint that empties it of its rulings and turns it into
general values without discipline.
Rigidity fears the question, is suspicious of reason, sanctifies
the means as it sanctifies the end, and turns religion into
memorized information, repeated forms, and practices
without effect.
Unrestraint, meanwhile, dreads commitment, invokes higher
purposes to demolish specific rulings, and invokes mercy to
disable obligation, turning religion into elastic slogans, vague
and general expressions, subject to popular taste, without
discipline or reference point. Both extremes do harm to
religion; however different their intentions may be.
True religion is neither a prison for the mind nor a pretext for
dissolution, but a precise scale that preserves the human being
from deviation while granting him, at the same time, the
capacity for movement and construction.
When religion is correctly understood, it does not halt at either
extreme, but is the religion of disciplined reason, living spirit,
and responsible action, a religion that opens the door to
questioning, not to trifling; that liberates reason without
severing its connection to revelation, freeing it from blind
imitation; and that liberates the spirit from anxiety, and
conduct from aimlessness. When it is misunderstood,
however, it turns into a heavy burden rather than a mercy.
Chapter 4: Islam Is the Religion of Innate Human Nature
b
and Reason Together
b
Among the greatest characteristics of Islam is that it does not
clash with human nature (fitrah), nor disable reason, nor
separate faith from thought. Islam did not address the human
being as a body alone, nor as a bare intellect, nor as an isolated
spirit, but addressed him as an integrated whole, addressing
the mind with proof, the heart with tranquillity, and conduct
with method. For this reason, its legislation came in harmony
with innate nature, stimulating to reason, and refining of
conduct.
There is no contradiction in Islam between faith and thought,
nor between submission and understanding, nor between
worship and work, and every attempt to separate these
elements is, in truth, a distortion of the reality of this religion.
When Islam is correctly understood, it does not stand as an
obstacle before progress but is a guide for it; it does not clash
with science but frames it with values; and it does not isolate
the human being from the world, but charges him with the
responsibility of reforming it.
This religion explains to the human being who he is, why he
was created, and to where he is journeying, granting him great
answers concerning existence, the purpose of existence,
responsibility, and destiny.
When the light of revelation meets the purity of innate nature
and the guidance of reason, the balanced human being arises,
one who worships Allah and understands life, who works for
this world while remaining connected to the Hereafter, and
who builds reality without losing his bearings. And here the
path begins: a path of conscious understanding, a living
religion, and a message capable of moving from the text to
reality, and from faith to civilization.
Conclusion of Part 1
b
The crisis of the contemporary Muslim is not a crisis of text,
but a crisis of understanding; it is not a crisis of religion, but a
crisis of awareness of religion. When Islam is reconnected
with its great function, religion returns to being a force of
construction, not a burden, a message for living, not a seasonal
ritual.
Understanding religion in an age of transformation does not
mean changing religion but returning to it as it was revealed,
with a conscious mind, a living heart, and an insightful view
of reality, and it is from this correct understanding that the
whole construction proceeds.
In the Parts to come, we shall proceed step by step in taking
apart this understanding and rebuilding it anew, upon the
foundation of revelation, the purposes of the Shari’ah, and the
reality of the new world.

intention is made sound; by it, worship is set upright; by it,
character is made firm; and by it, balance is restored in a
turbulent world.

b
The unseen (Al-ghayb) is that whose true reality is hidden
from the senses and the intellects, not because of any
deficiency in it, but because of the limitation of the human
being’s instruments in encompassing it. Allah has made faith
in the unseen the first of the believers’ qualities, saying:
“This

(Al-Baqarah

seeking to grasp their inner nature, are faith in Allah, the
Exalted; faith in divine decree and predestination; faith in the
Last Day; faith in the angels and the jinn; and faith in what
Allah and His Messenger have informed us of, of matters
beyond the reach of the senses.
This faith is not a faith of ignorance, but a faith of submission,
submission to Allah’s choice, and trust in His knowledge and
wisdom. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“It is not for a believing man
i

of intellectual mastery, and establishes the servitude of the
heart before the servitude of the intellect.

i
, both by Imam Al-
Ghazali.) This statement shows that knowledge is the path to
faith, that deed is the fruit of knowledge, and that knowledge
is of no benefit unless it bears the fruit of righteous action.
Reason here, then, is the raw material of faith, not its judge
over it, and reflection is a path to reverence, not a path to
doubt.
Chapter 3: The Increase and Decrease of Faith Between
b
Knowledge and Deed
b
Faith increases and decreases, a reality agreed upon among
the people of the Sunnah. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“That they
i
would increase [in] faith along with their [present] faith”
i
(Al-Fath
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Faith has over seventy branches, the highest
i
of which is the saying, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the lowest of
i
which is removing a harmful object from the road, and modesty
i
(haya’) is a branch of faith.”
i
(Reported by Muslim.)
Faith increases through increase in knowledge of Allah, His
names, and His attributes; reflection upon revelation and the
cosmos; righteous deeds; and the purification of the soul.
Faith decreases through ignorance and heedlessness; the
abandonment of righteous deeds; persistence in sin; and the
corruption of purpose and intention.
Al-Hasan Al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Faith is not by wishful thinking, nor by outward adornment,
but what settles firmly in the heart and is confirmed by deed.”
Chapter 4: Life Is Part of Faith
b
Faith is not a mental idea, nor an isolated emotional state, but
a way of life. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“Say, ‘Indeed, my prayer,
i
my rites of sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of
i
the worlds’”
i
Conduct, work, relationships, and daily choices, all of these
are branches among the branches of faith.
Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“The idea that never turns into conduct remains an illusion;
however, sound it may be [in theory].”
Chapter 5: Modesty (Haya’) Is Part of Faith
b
If faith unites the knowledge that guides the mind with the
submission that humbles the heart, then modesty (haya’) is the
fruit of this balance. It is not merely a social virtue, nor a
passing emotional reaction, but a station of faith reflecting
Allah’s presence in the heart, and His watchfulness in secret
and in the open.
The Prophet ﷺ joined modesty to faith as a part is joined to
the whole, saying:
“Modesty is a branch of faith,”
i
reported by
Abu ’Ubayd in his book
Al-Iman
i
; and in another narration:
“Modesty brings nothing but good,”
i
reported by Abu Dawud Al-
Tayalisi in his Musnad.
The concept of modesty in the balance of faith.
b
Modesty, in its true reality, is a breaking of the heart
before what is repugnant, despite one’s capacity to
commit it, an effect among the effects of magnifying
Allah, not a weakness or hesitancy. A person may refrain
from wrongdoing out of fear of people, and this is social
modesty; or out of fear of punishment, and this is external
deterrence; or out of a sense of shame before Allah, and
this is the modesty of faith. This last is proof that faith has
moved from being mere knowledge to becoming an
inward state and a practical conduct.
Modesty is the fruit of knowledge of Allah, Mighty and
b
Sublime.
b
The more a servant’s knowledge of Allah, the
Exalted, increases, of His names, His attributes, His
nearness, His knowledge, and His awareness, the more
his modesty before Him grows. Modesty is not ignorance,
but the result of knowledge. Some of the righteous
predecessors said: “Whoever truly knows Allah is truly
modest before Him.” From this we understand that
knowledge which produces no modesty is knowledge of
deficient effect, one that has not reached the heart.
Modesty is a station of submission, not a mere
b
character trait.
b
Modesty is not merely ethical refinement,
but an inward submission, a silent surrender to Allah’s
command. The modest servant abandons sin: not
because people see him, and not because the law forbids
it, but because his heart cannot bear to disobey the One
he reveres. This is the very essence of faith: to act as
though you see Allah, for even if you do not see Him, He
surely sees you.
The kinds of modesty and their relationship to faith.
b
Modesty may be distinguished into three levels: an
innate, instinctive modesty, which is a trait of character
and may be found in the believer and the non-believer
alike; an acquired, cultivated modesty, arising from
habits, customs, and environment; and a modesty of
faith, which is the one intended here, springing from
magnifying Allah and being conscious of His
watchfulness, increasing as faith increases and decreasing
as it decreases. For this reason, the departure of modesty
is a sign of a defect in faith, not merely in character.
There is no contradiction between modesty and
b
boldness in [defending] the truth.
b
Among the common
errors is to consider modesty a form of weakness or
hesitancy. The modesty of faith does not prevent one
from: speaking the truth; enjoining good; or showing
courage when it is called for. Rather, it prevents
shamelessness; transgression; and boldness against the
limits set by Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“If you feel no
i
shame, then do as you wish,”
i
reported by Ma’mar ibn
Rashid in his book
Al-Jami’
i
, meaning when modesty
departs, every restraint falls away with it.
The effect of modesty on conduct and uprightness.
b
Modesty of faith guards the limbs, disciplines the tongue,
refines intention, and prevents persistence in
wrongdoing. It is among the greatest causes of
uprightness free from both excess and harshness, for the
person who possesses it has no need of constant external
supervision, since their heart has already been filled with
an inward watchfulness.
Chapter Conclusion:
b
modesty is not a secondary virtue in
religion, but a precise indicator of the vitality of faith in the
heart. Whenever modesty weakens, it is a warning that faith
has become knowledge without effect, or awareness without
submission. And when knowledge that recognizes Allah,
submission that yields to Him, and modesty that prevents
disobeying Him are all united, the complete picture of a living
faith is realized, one that sets right both the heart and conduct
together.
Conclusion of Part 3
b
Faith is an unseen realm submitted to; a witnessed realm
reflected upon and understood; a knowledge that is put into
practice; a deed that is translated into action; and a life that is
lived.
Whoever combines submission in matters of the unseen,
reflection in matters of the witnessed, and action in reality, has
walked the path of uprightness, and has realized knowledge of
the self upon the guidance of revelation.
Part 4: Acts of Worship Between Form and Function
b
Introduction to Part 4:
b
the acts of worship were not legislated
in Islam to be bodily movements, or seasonal rituals cut off
from the reality of life, performed and then forgotten, nor
obligations discharged from one’s liability without leaving any
trace upon the soul or upon life.
Rather, the acts of worship were legislated to bring about an
inward transformation, to build a God-fearing human being,
to refine conduct, and to reorder the human being’s
relationship with his Lord, with himself, and with other
people, carrying the Muslim from one state to another, and
from one level of faith to a loftier one.
The command to worship was never an end, but a path to
realizing a conscious servitude that delivers the human being
from inner chaos and grants him a fixed moral compass in a
turbulent world.
When worship is emptied of its function, it turns from a force
of reform into an inherited habit, and from a message of
transformation into a seasonal practice that leaves no notable
trace upon conduct or values.
Having clarified, in the preceding Parts, the meaning and
reality of faith, and the effects of Islam upon the life of the
individual and society, we turn in this Part to a central issue
in which disorder frequently occurs in understanding the acts
of worship between their outward form and their inward
function.
The acts of worship in Islam were not legislated merely for the
performance of bodily movements or verbal utterances but
were legislated to realize tremendous purposes: building the
human being from within, purifying the soul, disciplining
conduct, and binding the servant to his Lord in every affair of
his life.
First: the problem of separating form from function.
b
Some
Muslim societies have become afflicted with a merely formal
performance of the acts of worship, with a weakening of their
effects on character and transactions, such that one finds a
person who prays, yet whose prayer does not restrain him
from indecency and wrongdoing; who fasts, yet whose fasting
leaves no imprint on his tongue or his conduct; who performs
the pilgrimage, then returns as he was before; who observes
the rites, without their bearing fruit in uprightness, awareness,
or a sense of responsibility.
Thus, many acts of worship have become bodily movements
devoid of spirit. Here, the disorder does not lie in the act of
worship itself, but in the understanding of it, in one’s presence
of heart within it, and in its purposes. This disorder does not
go back to any deficiency in the legislation, but to a poor
understanding and application, since worship has, for some,
turned from a means of purification and construction into a
repeated habit empty of spirit and purpose.
Second: the concept of form and function in acts of worship
b
performed daily, weekly, or yearly.
b
1. Form is the outward shape of the act of worship, its
pillars, conditions, and manner, and this is required, for
the act of worship is not valid without it.
2. Function is the purpose for which the act of worship was
legislated: God-consciousness (Taqwa), discipline,
purification, uprightness, and the reform of the individual
and society.
The Islamic method does not accept a separation between the
two; rather, it rests upon realizing the correct form while
keeping the intended function ever in mind. Allah, the
Exalted, says:
“Their meat will not reach Allah, nor will their blood,
i
but what reaches Him is piety from you”
i
(Al-Hajj 22:37).
Third: the importance of this Part in building the true
b
Muslim who understands his religion.
b
The importance of
this Part flows from the fact that it restores the correction of
the concept of formal worship into conscious religiosity and
shows that the acts of worship are instruments of
transformation and reform, not frozen rituals.
Fourth: the method of this Part.
b
This Part will address, Allah
willing, the essential acts of worship in Islam, such as prayer,
zakat, fasting, and pilgrimage, not merely from the angle of
formal performance, but from the angle of understanding,
function, and effect. We shall consider each act of worship in
its correct legal form, its educational and doctrinal function,
and its behavioural, social, economic, and cultural effects,
exposing the disorder present in its understanding or its
practice, and clarifying the gap between the purpose for which
it was legislated and what it has become, for many people
today, in practice. This Part contains four chapters and a
conclusion.
Chapter 1: Why Were Acts of Worship Legislated?
b
The fundamental principle regarding the acts of worship is
that they are instruments of formation before they are outward
expressions of commitment. Allah, the Exalted, says, stating
the comprehensive purpose of worship:
“O mankind, worship
i
your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may
i
become righteous”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:21), the great goal, then, is
God-consciousness (Taqwa), and God-consciousness is not
merely a word to be uttered, but a state of awareness,
watchfulness, and inward discipline.
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“And I did not create the jinn and
i
mankind except to worship Me”
i
(Adh-Dhariyat 51:56). Ibn
Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him), in his exegesis, said
this means that they may profess His oneness, submit to Him,
and humble themselves before Him in obedience.
Worship reorders the human being’s relationship with his
Lord, liberates him from false servitudes, and grants him a
lasting moral compass.
Shaykh Al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on
him) said: “Worship is a comprehensive term for everything
Allah loves and is pleased with, of sayings and deeds, outward
and inward.” (See:
Majmu’ Al-Fatawa
i
by Shaykh Al-Islam Ibn
Taymiyyah.)
Worship, then, is not confined to the mosque, nor cut off from
life, but extends to encompass intention, conduct, dealings,
and work.
Chapter 2: Acts of Worship and the Building of the
b
Balanced Human Being
b
Among the wisdoms of Allah, the Exalted, is that He
distributed the acts of worship across the limbs, the hearts, and
the times and seasons, so that no one dimension might
overwhelm the others. Worship in Islam purifies the spirit,
disciplines the self, and sets conduct upright. Allah, the
Exalted, says:
“He has certainly succeeded who purifies it [the soul],
i
and he has certainly failed who instils it [with corruption]”
i
(Ash-
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“Indeed, within the body there is
i
a morsel of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is
i
corrupt, the whole body is corrupt, indeed, it is the heart.”
i
(Agreed
upon.) The acts of worship, then, are not a mere accumulation
of deeds, but a reform of the seat of command: the heart.
Imam Al-Ghazali (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The
deeds of the limbs avail nothing unless they revive the deeds
of the heart.” (See:
Ihya’ ’Ulum Al-Din
i
, chapter on the secrets
of prayer.)
For this reason, the Prophet ﷺ always linked worship to
conduct, as in his saying:
“O Mu’adh, be conscious of Allah
i
wherever you are, follow a bad deed with a good one that will erase it,
i
and treat people with good character.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tirmidhi.)
The true fruit of worship, then, is the balanced human being
who worships Allah, does good to His creation, and
disciplines himself.
Chapter 3: When Worship Is Severed from Its Effect
b
Among the gravest afflictions besetting religiosity today is that
worship turns into mere habit and loses its capacity for
transformation. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“So woe to those who
i
pray, [but] who are heedless of their prayer”
i
Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: “They
are those who delay it past its proper time, or do not perform
it as it should be performed.” (See the exegeses of Imam Ibn
Jarir Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir.)
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“How many a fasting person gains nothing
i
from his fast but hunger and thirst.”
i
(Reported by Ibn Majah in
his Sunan.)
This indicates that worship without presence, without
understanding, and without struggle against the self, may
remain merely an outward form devoid of spirit.
Al-Hasan Al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Faith is not by wishful thinking, nor by outward adornment,
but what settles firmly in the heart and is confirmed by deed.”
(See:
Al-Musannaf
i
by Ibn Abi Shaybah.) This statement
means: faith is not mere speech or wishful thinking but must
reside in the heart and be translated into deeds.
When worship becomes severed from its effect, people lose
confidence in religiosity, religion turns into a heavy burden,
and the door opens to hypocrisy or aversion. The greatest
danger is that a person may imagine himself close to Allah
through his prayer, his fasting, his remembrance, and his
recitation of the Qur’an, while in truth he is far from Him in
his conduct, his character, and his dealings.
Chapter 4: Worship, A Force of Inner Transformation
b
When worship is performed with awareness, it becomes an
energy for reform, a source of strength, and a motive for
commitment. Allah, the Exalted, says of prayer:
“Indeed,
i
prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing”
i
(Al-’Ankabut
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Whoever does not abandon false speech and
i
acting upon it, and ignorant behaviour, Allah has no need of his
i
leaving his food and drink.”
i
(Reported by Al-Bukhari.)
True worship changes the way a person thinks, reorders his
desires, and strengthens his will in the face of appetite.
Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Servitude (’ubudiyyah) is the perfection of love joined with
the perfection of submission, and the heart is not set right
except by this.” (See:
Madarij Al-Salikin
i
by Imam Ibn Al-
Qayyim.)
When the Muslim comes to understand why he worships,
how he worships, and what ought to change in him after
worship, the acts of worship transform from heavy obligations
into stations of construction and purification.
Conclusion of Part 4
b
The acts of worship in Islam are not intended for their own
sake alone, but for what they produce within the human being.
Every act of worship that does not set the heart right, does not
refine conduct, and does not bring one nearer to Allah, is an
act of worship in need of a review of its understanding, not of
its abandonment.
From here we move from worship as mere form to worship as
effect, and from ritual to transformation.
Part 5: Prayer, the Bond of Life, a Permanent Connection,
b
not a Temporary Duty
b
Introduction to Part 5:
b
prayer is not merely an obligation to
be discharged, nor repeated movements performed at fixed
times, but a daily, ever-renewed relationship between the
servant and his Lord, one that resets the heart, straightens
conduct, and grants the human being the capacity to remain
firm in a turbulent world. If prayer is sound, the scale of life is
set upright; if it is corrupted, everything is disturbed.
In its true reality, prayer is not a temporary spiritual respite,
but a system of permanent connection between the servant
and his Lord, resetting the heart five times a day, amid the
noise of life and the entanglement of worldly interests. Allah,
the Exalted, says:
“And establish prayer for My remembrance”
i
(Ta-Ha 20:14), the remembrance of Allah is the very essence
of prayer, and it is what grants prayer its capacity to restore
inward balance. This Part contains four chapters and a
conclusion.
Chapter 1: Prayer in the Balance of Faith
b
Allah made prayer the pillar of religion, and the first thing the
servant will be asked about on the Day of Resurrection. The
Prophet ﷺ said:
“The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer,
i
and the peak of its hump is jihad.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tirmidhi,
who said it is a sound, authentic hadith.)
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“The first matter the servant will be brought
i
to account for on the Day of Resurrection is his prayer: if it is sound,
i
the rest of his deeds are sound, and if it is corrupt, the rest of his deeds
i
are corrupt.”
i
(Reported by Abu Dawud Al-Tayalisi in his
Musnad and Al-Tabarani in
Al-Mu’jam Al-Awsat
i
, and graded
sound by several scholars.)
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“And establish prayer and do not be of
i
those who associate others with Allah”
i
(Ar-Rum 30:31), Allah
thereby linked prayer to monotheism, and made its
abandonment among the greatest gateways to deviation.
’Umar ibn Al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said:
“There is no share in Islam for one who abandons prayer.”
(See:
Al-Musannaf
i
by Ibn Abi Shaybah, and
Al-Muwatta’
i
of
Imam Malik.)
Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “Prayer
is the pillar of Islam; whoever demolishes it has demolished
religion.” (See:
Kitab Al-Salah
i
by Imam Ahmad.)
Prayer, then, is not a secondary branch, but the centre of
gravity of faith in the Muslim’s life. Prayer that does not renew
faith, does not set character right, and does not soften the
hardness of the heart, is a prayer performed only in form, from
which the function has been absent.
Chapter 2: The Philosophy of Repetition and Temporal
b
Discipline
b
Among the wisdoms of Allah, the Exalted, is that He made
prayer obligatory five times in the day and night, so that it
might be a continuous renewal of faith, or a wireless network,
as it were, connecting the servant to his Creator, Mighty and
Sublime, without interruption.
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“So maintain prayer. Indeed, prayer has
i
been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times”
i
(An-Nisa’
4:103), prayer, then, organizes time, trains the soul in
discipline, and binds the human being to heaven amid the
crowded press of the earth.
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“What do you think, if there were a river at
i
the door of one of you, in which he bathed five times every day, would
i
any trace of dirt remain on him?” They said, “No trace of dirt would
i
remain on him.” He said, “That is the likeness of the five prayers:
i
Allah erases sins by them.”
i
(Agreed upon.)
Imam Ibn Rajab Al-Hanbali (may Allah have mercy on him)
said: “Repeated prayer purifies the heart just as water purifies
the body.” (See:
Al-Khushu’ fi Al-Salah
i
by Imam Ibn Rajab Al-
Hanbali.)
Repetition in prayer, then, is not a tiresome repetition, but an
educational mercy, for the human being weakens and grows
heedless.
Chapter 3: The Effect of Prayer on Conduct and Character
b
Allah did not make prayer an end, but a means to the reform
of conduct. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“And establish prayer.
i
Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing”
i
(Al-
’Ankabut 29:45). Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him),
in his exegesis, said this means that prayer, containing as it
does the remembrance of Allah, restrains its performer from
acts of disobedience.
Ibn Abi Hatim related in his exegesis, on the authority of
’Imran ibn Husayn, who said: “The Prophet ﷺ was asked
about the meaning of Allah’s words, ‘Indeed, prayer prohibits
immorality and wrongdoing.’ He said, ‘Whoever’s prayer
does not restrain him from immorality and wrongdoing has
no [true] prayer.’” (Reported by Al-Tabarani in
Al-Mu’jam
i
and Sa’id ibn Mansur in his Sunan.) The scholars said this
means there is no complete prayer [in such a case].
True prayer refines the tongue, restrains appetite, that is,
governs and curbs it, or reduces its influence, and revives the
conscience. Al-Hasan Al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on
him) said: “Prayer, for whoever truly performs it, restrains
from immorality and wrongdoing.” (See: the exegesis of Ibn
Kathir, and
Al-Durr Al-Manthur
i
by Al-Suyuti.) This means: a
prayer complete in its pillars and its humility is what restrains
its performer from immorality and wrongdoing.
If you see one who prays yet commits injustice, lies, or betrays
trust, then know that the flaw is not in the prayer, but in the
absence of the heart and a failure to understand worship.
Chapter 4: Why Does Prayer Sometimes Fail to Bring
b
About Change?
b
This is a candid question that must be asked, for reality bears
witness that many people pray without their lives ever
changing. There are many reasons for this, among the most
important:
The absence of humility (khushu’).
b
Allah, the Exalted,
says:
“In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most
i
Merciful. Certainly, will the believers have succeeded, they who
i
are during their prayer humbly submissive”
i
(Al-Mu’minun
23:1–2). The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Indeed, a man may finish his
i
prayer, and nothing has been recorded for him of it but a tenth
i
of it, or a ninth, or an eighth, or a seventh, or a sixth, or a fifth,
i
or a quarter, or a third, or a half.”
i
(Reported by Abu Dawud
in his Sunan.)
Performing prayer as a habit, not as an act of worship.
b
Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “A
prayer that produces neither reverence nor restraint from
wrongdoing is a prayer in form only, without its true
reality.” (See:
Al-Jawab Al-Kafi
i
by Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim.)
This means: a prayer that neither increases humility nor
prevents wrongdoing more closely resembles mere
movements than a true prayer.
Failure to understand what is recited within the prayer.
b
Shaykh Al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy
on him) said: “Among the greatest causes of the heart’s
presence is understanding the meanings of what the one
praying recites.” (See:
Majmu’ Al-Fatawa
i
by Shaykh Al-
Islam Ibn Taymiyyah.) This means understanding the
meanings of the Qur’an and the remembrances recited in
prayer is among the most important causes of the heart’s
presence and its humility.
A weakness in struggle after the prayer.
b
Allah, the
Exalted, says:
“And seek help through patience and prayer,
i
and indeed, it is difficult except for the humbly submissive [to
i
Allah]”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:45). Prayer assists, but it does not
dispense with continued struggle against the self.
Conclusion of Part 5
b
Prayer is not merely a temporary connection, but a complete
connection to life itself; it is the balance of faith, the school of
discipline, the engine of character, and the source of firmness
in an age of trials. Whoever wishes to reform his life should
begin by reforming his prayer, in understanding, in presence,
and in conduct.
Part 6: Zakat, the Economy of Mercy, the Worship of
b
Wealth, and the Purification of Society
b
Introduction to Part 6:
b
Islam did not make wealth a god to be
worshipped, nor an evil to be shunned, but a means of
stewardship and a trial, by which the sincerity of faith is
measured, and the balance of society is built.
Zakat is not an optional charity, nor a social tax, but one of
the pillars of religion, a rite of profound civilizational effect,
purifying the soul of the disease of miserliness and
redistributing mercy within society.
When zakat is discharged as Allah intended, the doors of
class-based resentment are closed, poverty is contained, and
society becomes settled. When zakat is neglected, wealth
becomes detached from values, trust collapses, and social
bonds are severed. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“There is no possessor of
i
hoarded wealth who does not pay its zakat, but it will be heated in the
i
fire of Hell [and used to brand him].”
i
(Reported by Muslim.)
When zakat turns into a figure paid without awareness, it loses
a great part of its educational and social effect, remaining
legally valid while deficient in effect. This Part contains four
chapters and a conclusion.
Chapter 1: Wealth Between Stewardship and Ownership
b
Islam sets right, from the outset, the concept of wealth, so that
the human being is not left to wander between greed and
deprivation. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“And give them from the
i
wealth of Allah which He has given you”
i
(An-Nur 24:33), wealth,
then, belongs to Allah in its creation, and to the human being
in his acquisition of it; it is a trust before it is a possession.
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“Believe in Allah and His Messenger and
i
spend out of that in which He has made you successors [i.e.,
i
stewards]”
i
(Al-Hadid 57:7).
Imam Al-Qurtubi (may Allah have mercy on him) said, in his
exegesis: “In this verse is proof that wealth is not, in true
reality, owned by us, but that we are made stewards over it.”
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“The feet of a servant will not move on the
i
Day of Resurrection until he is asked about four things: about his life,
i
how he spent it; about his youth, how he wore it out; about his wealth,
i
whence he acquired it and how he spent it; and about his knowledge,
i
what he did with it.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tirmidhi.)
Zakat, then, resets the human being’s relationship with
wealth, and liberates him from servitude to it.
Chapter 2: Zakat as an Instrument of Social Justice
b
Allah, the Exalted, has linked zakat to prayer in dozens of
places in His Book, to show that faith is not complete without
social justice. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“And establish prayer and
i
give zakat and bow with those who bow [in worship and obedience]”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:43). He has clarified its designated recipients
with precision, saying:
“Zakat expenditures are only for the poor
i
and for the needy and for those employed to collect [zakat] and for
i
bringing hearts together [for Islam] and for freeing captives [or slaves]
i
and for those in debt and for the cause of Allah and for the [stranded]
i
traveller, an obligation [imposed] by Allah. And Allah is Knowing
i
and Wise”
i
(At-Tawbah 9:60).
Imam Ibn ’Ashur (may Allah have mercy on him) said, in his
exegesis
Al-Tahrir wa’l-Tanwir
i
: “Zakat is a complete social
system aiming to preserve the balance of society.”
It is related from Ibn Abbas that Mu’adh said:
“The Messenger
i
of Allah (cid:0) sent me and said: ‘You are going to a people of the
i
Scripture. Invite them first to testify that there is no god but Allah and
i
that I am the Messenger of Allah. If they obey that, then inform them
i
that Allah has made five prayers obligatory upon them in every day
i
and night. If they obey that, then inform them that Allah has made
i
charity obligatory upon them, to be taken from their rich and given to
i
their poor. If they obey that, then beware of [taking] the best of their
i
wealth, and beware of the supplication of the one wronged, for there
i
is no barrier between it and Allah.’”
i
(Agreed upon.) Zakat, then,
is not a mere favour, but an established right, one that
safeguards the dignity of society and purifies the soul of the
wealthy.
Chapter 3: The Effects of Neglecting Zakat in Societies
b
When zakat is disabled, it is not only the economy that is
disturbed, but values that collapse. Allah, the Exalted, warns
those who withhold zakat, saying:
“And those who hoard gold
i
and silver and spend it not in the way of Allah, give them tidings of a
i
painful punishment”
i
(At-Tawbah 9:34).
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“No people withhold zakat, but
i
Allah afflicts them with years of drought.”
i
(Reported by Al-
Tabarani in
Al-Mu’jam Al-Awsat
i
Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: “By Allah, I
shall surely fight whoever separates prayer from zakat, for
zakat is the due of wealth. By Allah, if they withhold from me
[even] a young she-goat that they used to render to the
Messenger of Allah ﷺ, I would fight them for withholding it.”
’Umar then said: “By Allah, it was only that I saw that Allah
had opened Abu Bakr’s breast to fight, and I recognized that
it was the truth.” (Reported by ’Abd Al-Razzaq in his
Musannaf.)
Imam Al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The
disabling of zakat portends the collapse of the social purposes
of the Shari’ah.” (See:
Al-Muwafaqat fi Usul Al-Shari’ah
i
by
Imam Al-Shatibi.) This means: the failure to pay zakat
threatens the realization of the social objectives of Islamic law.
The absence of zakat leads to the intensification of poverty,
the accumulation of wealth in the hands of a few, the spread
of social resentment, and a weakening sense of belonging.
Chapter 4: Mutual Solidarity, the Foundation of
b
Civilizational Stability
b
Civilizations are not built on production alone, but on justice
and mutual mercy. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“Take, [O
i
Muhammad], from their wealth a charity by which you purify them
i
and cause them increase, and invoke [Allah’s blessings] upon them”
i
(At-Tawbah 9:103).
Zakat purifies wealth, purifies the soul, and builds bridges of
trust. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“The believers, in their mutual love,
i
mercy, and compassion, are like a single body: when one part of it
i
complains [of illness], the rest of the body responds to it with
i
wakefulness and fever.”
i
(Agreed upon.)
Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Zakat is among the greatest causes of the soundness of
wealth, and of preserving societies from ruin.” (See:
Al-Wabil
i
Al-Sayyib
i
by Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim.) This means zakat is
among the most important causes that purify wealth and
increase its blessing.
When society discharges its zakat, crime diminishes, souls
settle, and a sense of shared destiny grows stronger, and this is
the very essence of the economy of mercy.
Conclusion of Part 6
b
Zakat is not merely a financial act of worship, but a project of
justice, a system of social security, and a civilizational
balance. If we desire settled societies, a humane economy, and
a sincere religiosity, then zakat must return from a neglected
line item to the very heart of the Islamic system.
Part 7: Fasting, Rebuilding the Human Being, and a
b
School for Disciplining the Will
b
Introduction to Part 7:
b
fasting, in its true reality, is not merely
abstention from food and drink, nor a passing seasonal act of
worship, but a profound program of formation, reordering the
human being’s inward life: his desires, his will, his awareness,
and his conscience.
It is a comprehensive educational program, teaching the soul
the meaning of mastery rather than submission [to appetite].
In a world governed by desire, and fed by haste, in which the
human being is measured by what he consumes, fasting comes
to say to him: you are greater than your desire, stronger than
your appetite, and loftier than your momentary life. This Part
contains four chapters and a conclusion.
Chapter 1: Fasting and the Liberation of the Will
b
The first evident purpose of fasting is to build a free will,
enslaved neither by appetite nor by habit. Allah, the Exalted,
says:
“O you who have believed, decreed upon you is fasting as it was
i
decreed upon those before you, that you may become righteous”
i
(Al-
Baqarah 2:183).
Allah thus made the great purpose of fasting to be God-
consciousness (Taqwa), and it is the fruit of awareness,
discipline, and watchfulness.
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“O assembly of young men, whoever among
i
you is able to marry, let him marry, for it is more restraining of the
i
gaze and more protective of chastity; and whoever is unable, let him
i
fast, for it is a shield for him.”
i
(Agreed upon.) That is: fasting
restrains sexual appetite and strengthens one’s mastery over
the self.
Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“In fasting there is a subduing of the self, a breaking of its
dominance, and a reminder to it of its own weakness and its
need for Allah.” (See:
Zad Al-Ma’ad
i
by Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim.)
This means there is, in fasting, a restraint of the self and a
training of it to abandon its desires.
Fasting, then, is a school of inward strength, not bodily
weakness, nor mere deprivation of food and drink.
Chapter 2: Purifying the Soul in the School of Ramadan
b
Ramadan is not a month of mere abstention, but a month of
comprehensive purification. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“He has
i
certainly succeeded who purifies it [the soul]”
i
(Ash-Shams 91:9).
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and in
i
expectation of reward, his previous sins will be forgiven.”
i
(Agreed
upon.) He also said:
“When Ramadan comes, the gates of Paradise
i
are opened, the gates of Hell are closed, and the devils are chained.”
i
(Agreed upon.)
Imam Al-Ghazali (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The
true reality of fasting is the restraint of the limbs from sin, and
of the heart from base ambitions.” (See:
Ihya’ ’Ulum Al-Din
i
by
Imam Al-Ghazali.) Imam Al-Ghazali, may Allah the Exalted
have mercy on him, states in
Ihya’ ’Ulum Al-Din
i
that fasting is
of three degrees:
The fasting of the common people:
b
restraining the
stomach and the private parts, and all the other bodily
faculties, from satisfying appetite.
The fasting of the elect:
b
restraining the hearing, the
sight, the tongue, the hand, the foot, and the other limbs
from sin.
The fasting of the elect of the elect:
b
restraining the heart
from base concerns and worldly preoccupations.
Al-Hasan Al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Allah has made Ramadan a racecourse for His servants, in
which they compete with one another in obedience to Him.”
(See:
Ihya’ ’Ulum Al-Din
i
by Imam Al-Ghazali.) This means:
Ramadan is an arena for worshippers, in which they compete
for obedience and God-consciousness, some race ahead and
are victorious, and some lag and lose.
Ramadan, then, awakens the conscience, softens the heart,
and intensifies self-examination.
Chapter 3: Fasting and Resisting Consumerism and
b
Appetite
b
In an age of excessive consumption, fasting comes to break
this cycle. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Fasting is a shield”
i
(Agreed
upon), that is, a protection from appetite, from anger, and
from behavioural excess.
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“When one of you is fasting, let him not use
i
obscene speech, nor act in ignorance; and if someone fights him or
i
insults him, let him say, ‘I am fasting.’”
i
(Agreed upon.)
Ibn Rajab Al-Hanbali (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Fasting narrows the pathways of Satan and prevents the
expansion of appetite.” (See:
Lata’if Al-Ma’arif
i
by Imam Ibn
Rajab Al-Hanbali.) This means fasting narrows Satan’s
pathways within the human being, weakening his whispers
and diminishing his influence.
Fasting, then, trains a person in contentment, curbs
extravagance, and restores due regard for values, and for this
reason fasting was a civilizational tool before it was an
individual act of worship.
Chapter 4: Why Do Some People Leave Ramadan
b
Unchanged?
b
This painful question exposes a defect in understanding and
in practice. Among the most prominent causes:
Reducing fasting to mere hunger
b
, that is, treating fasting
as nothing more than abstention from food and drink.
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“How many a fasting person gains
i
nothing from his fast but hunger and thirst.”
i
(Reported by Ibn
Majah.)
A weakness in the heart’s watchfulness.
b
Allah, the
Exalted, says:
“Indeed, Allah is ever, over you, an Observer”
i
(An-Nisa’ 4:1).
The absence of continuity after Ramadan.
b
Allah, the
Exalted, says:
“And worship your Lord until there comes to
i
your certainty [i.e., death]”
i
(Al-Hijr 15:99).
Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “Among
the signs of an accepted deed is that it bears the fruit of a
righteous deed after it.” (See:
Madarij Al-Salikin
i
by Imam Ibn
Al-Qayyim.) This means among the signs that a righteous
deed has been accepted is that it is followed by another
righteous deed, for a righteous deed draws further righteous
deeds in its wake.
The great function of fasting is God-consciousness (Taqwa),
and this is an inward discipline that accompanies the human
being after Ramadan, not only during it.
Fasting, then, is not a temporal end, but a point of departure
toward a better state.
Conclusion of Part 7
b
Fasting rebuilds the will, purifies the soul, and liberates the
human being from consumption. If the Muslim emerges from
Ramadan with a stronger will, a purer heart, and more
disciplined conduct, then fasting has fulfilled its function; if
not, the review that is required is not of the fast itself, but of
one’s understanding of it.
Part 8: Hajj, the Nation in a Single Scene, for the Building
b
of Unity
b
Introduction to Part 8:
b
the Hajj is not an individual spiritual
journey, nor a seasonal rite of limited effect, but a global event
of faith, in which hearts meet before bodies, in which
differences dissolve, and in which the very meaning of
“nation” (ummah) is reformulated.
In the Hajj, the human being sheds every mark of distinction
and dons the pure garment of servitude, moving within a
congregation defined by neither homeland nor colour, but by
creed and a single direction of prayer alone.
It is not merely an individual journey of faith, but a project of
grand unity: to stand as a servant of Allah alongside millions
of Allah’s servants, in the best of seasons, in the most sacred
of lands, in the presence of the finest of Allah’s servants, the
guests of the Most Merciful. In it, the message of Hajj is made
manifest in building a collective consciousness, a sense of
shared destiny, and a responsibility for reform. This Part
contains four chapters and a conclusion.
Chapter 1: Hajj Between Rite and Purpose
b
Allah, the Exalted, has made clear that Hajj is not a movement
without purpose, but an act of worship with manifest aims.
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“And [due] to Allah from the people is a
i
pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find thereto a way”
i
(Aal ’Imran 3:97).
He, the Exalted, also says:
“That they may witness benefits for
i
themselves”
i
(Al-Hajj 22:28). Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy
on him), in his exegesis, said: these benefits encompass both
religious and worldly good.
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“An accepted Hajj has no reward but
i
Paradise.”
i
(Agreed upon.)
Hajj, then, binds the servant to monotheism, trains him in
absolute obedience, and instils in him the meaning of
compliance with the commands of Allah, the Exalted.
Imam Al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “Hajj
gathers together the greatest purposes of the Shari’ah.” (See:
Al-Muwafaqat
i
by Imam Al-Shatibi.) This means: Hajj brings
together the most important purposes of Islamic law.
Chapter 2: The Unity of the Nation in a Single Garment
b
Among the greatest scenes of the Hajj is the shedding of
distinctions of class, race, colour, dress, and affiliation. The
Prophet ﷺ said:
“Indeed, Allah does not look at your outward forms,
i
nor at your bodies, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.”
i
(Reported by Muslim.)
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“O people, indeed your Lord is one, and indeed
i
your father [Adam] is one. There is no superiority of an Arab over a
i
non-Arab, nor of a non-Arab over an Arab, nor of a red [-skinned
i
person] over a black one, nor of a black one over a red one, except by
i
God-consciousness.”
i
(Reported by Imam Ahmad and ’Abdullah
ibn Al-Mubarak in his Musnad.)
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight
i
of Allah is the most righteous of you”
i
(Al-Hujurat 49:13). Imam
Al-Nawawi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “In the
pilgrim’s state of ritual consecration (ihram) there is a
reminder of the equality of all creation.” (See:
Al-Majmu’ Sharh
i
Al-Muhadhdhab
i
by Imam Al-Nawawi.)
This means: the state of ihram reminds Muslims of their
equality with one another, for those in the state of
consecration are equal in their simple garments of ihram,
without distinction between rich or poor, great or small,
African or American, European or Asian.
Hajj, then, redefines identity, corrects the scale of distinction,
and cultivates brotherhood.
Chapter 3: Hajj, A Global Congress of Faith
b
In the Hajj, Muslims gather from every distant corner,
carrying with them concerns, questions, and challenges.
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“And proclaim to the people the Hajj;
i
they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from
i
every distant pass”
i
(Al-Hajj 22:27). Allah, the Exalted, also says:
“Indeed this, your religion, is one religion, and I am your Lord, so
i
worship Me”
i
(Al-Anbiya 21:92).
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“The believer to the believer is like a structure,
i
parts of which support other parts,”
i
and he interlaced his fingers.
(Agreed upon.)
Imam Muhammad Rashid Rida (may Allah have mercy on
him) said: “Hajj is the greatest annual Islamic congress; where
it put to good use, it would transform the nation.” (See:
Manasik Al-Hajj: Ahkamuhu wa Hikamuhu
i
by Imam
Muhammad Rashid Rida.) This means it affirms the
importance of Hajj in uniting Muslims and strengthening
Islamic solidarity and considers Hajj an opportunity for the
exchange of ideas and cooperation among Muslims.
Hajj is thus an opportunity for acquaintance, and a field for
the exchange of experiences, opinions, resources, and
expertise, and a reminder of a shared destiny.
Chapter 4: Civilizational Lessons from the Rites of Hajj
b
Every rite of the Hajj carries a profound civilizational lesson
for the Islamic nation, wherever its members may be and
wherever they may be found in the world:
The circumambulation of the House (tawaf):
b
Allah, the
Exalted, says:
“And let them circumambulate the ancient House”
i
(Al-Hajj 22:29). Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on
him) said: “In the circumambulation is a declaration that
Allah is the centre of life.” (See:
Zad Al-Ma’ad
i
by Imam Ibn
Al-Qayyim.) This means circumambulating the Ka’bah is a
declaration of Allah’s centrality in the Muslim’s life and
affirms the importance of circumambulation in strengthening
one’s love for Allah and attachment to Him.
The going back and forth between Safa and Marwah (sa’i):
b
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“Indeed, Safa and Marwah are among
i
the symbols of Allah. So, whoever makes Hajj to the House or
i
performs ’umrah, there is no blame upon him for walking between
i
them”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:158). Imam Ibn Kathir (may Allah have
mercy on him) said, in his exegesis, that the sa’i is an
emulation of the Lady Hagar, and a training in taking up the
means [to one’s ends].
Standing at ’Arafah:
b
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Hajj is ’Arafah.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tirmidhi.) Imam Ibn Rajab Al-Hanbali (may
Allah have mercy on him) said: “The Day of ’Arafah is a scene
that recalls the Day of Gathering [i.e., the Day of
Judgement].” (See:
Lata’if Al-Ma’arif
i
by Imam Ibn Rajab Al-
Hanbali.) This means: the Day of ’Arafah is a magnificent
scene in which the human being is reminded of the Day of
Gathering and its terrors, and it affirms the importance of the
Day of ’Arafah in the forgiveness of sins and liberation from
the Fire.
Spending the night at Muzdalifah:
b
this reminds the pilgrims
of the true reality of patience and obedience, of cooperation
and mutual mercy, and of equality among themselves. All of
them spend the night sleeping upon the ground, and their
sleeping side by side reminds them of the grave, where no
distinction is made between rich and poor, ruler and ruled,
slave and free.
The stoning of the pillars (rami Al-jamarat):
b
this reminds the
pilgrims of defiance and steadfastness, our master Abraham
defied Satan and stoned him with pebbles, and of unity and
gathering, as millions of Muslims cast stones with a single
purpose and a single united act, and of ridding oneself of evil,
for the stoning of the pillars is a symbol of casting off desires
and evil whisperings, and of obedience to Allah, for the
stoning of the pillars expresses obedience to Allah and the
carrying out of His commands.
Hajj, then, binds this world to the next, deed to reliance upon
Allah, and the individual to the nation, and is a tremendous
opportunity for acquaintance and the exchange of experience
and knowledge, as well as both worldly and otherworldly
benefits.
Conclusion of Part 8
b
Hajj is not an individual journey, but a declaration of
nationhood, a renewal of covenant, and the building of a
collective consciousness. Whoever performs the Hajj and
returns humble, unburdened of pretension, and aware of his
responsibility toward the nation, has fulfilled the function of
the Hajj.
Part 9: Islam and the System of Contemporary Life
b
Introduction to Part 9:
b
Islam did not come to be an isolated
spiritual rite, nor a devotional system confined to the mosque,
but came as comprehensive guidance, organizing the human
being’s relationship with his Lord, with himself, with others,
and with the world around him.
With the complexity of contemporary life, and the
intertwining of politics, economics, science, and technology,
the question renews itself: does Islam possess a vision for
modern life? The answer is neither a defence nor a
justification, but a historical and religious truth: that Islam is
fit for every time and place, because it engages with the human
being, whether male or female, young or old, slave or free, rich
or poor, ruler or ruled, learned or ignorant, resident or
traveller, before it engages with particulars. This Part contains
four chapters and a conclusion.
Chapter 1: Islam and Knowledge
b
From the very first verse revealed, Islam placed knowledge at
the heart of its civilizational project. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“Read in the name of your Lord who created”
i
(Al-’Alaq 96:1).
Allah, the Exalted, also says:
“Say, ‘Are those who know equal to
i
those who do not know?’”
i
(Az-Zumar 39:9), and He, the Exalted,
says:
“Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have
i
knowledge”
i
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon
i
every Muslim.”
i
(Reported by Ibn Majah in his Sunan, and
graded sound by the scholars.)
Imam Al-Ghazali (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him)
said: “Knowledge is the root of happiness, and from it deeds
spring forth.” (See:
Ihya’ ’Ulum Al-Din
i
by Imam Al-Ghazali.)
This means knowledge is the root of happiness, and righteous
deeds spring from correct knowledge, and it affirms the
importance of knowledge in the reform of the self and the
improvement of one’s deeds.
Imam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Religion does not oppose sound knowledge; rather, it bears
witness to it and guides it.” (See:
Majmu’ Al-Fatawa
i
by Shaykh
Al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah.) This means: the religion of Islam
does not conflict with sound knowledge but bears witness to it
and guides it toward the truth, and it affirms the importance
of harmony between sound knowledge and the religion of
Islam.
Islam, then, does not fear knowledge, nor is it hostile to
reason, but disciplines knowledge with values.
Chapter 2: Islam and the Economy
b
Islam did not leave wealth without direction, nor the economy
without ethics. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“But seek, through that
i
which Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and [yet], do
i
not forget your share of the world”
i
(Al-Qasas 28:77).
Allah, the Exalted, also says:
“But Allah has permitted trade and
i
has forbidden interest”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:275).
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“The truthful, trustworthy merchant will be
i
with the prophets, the truthful, and the martyrs.”
i
(Reported by Al-
Tirmidhi.)
Imam Ibn Khaldun (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Transactions in the Shari’ah are built upon securing benefit
and repelling harm.” (See:
Al-Muqaddimah
i
by Ibn Khaldun.)
This statement affirms the importance of taking public
interests into account, and of avoiding harm, within Islamic
law.
The economy in Islam, then, is production without
oppression, earning without exploitation, and mutual
solidarity that does not efface the individual.
Chapter 3: Islam and Society
b
Islam came to build a cohesive society founded upon justice,
mercy, and responsibility. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“Indeed,
i
Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives”
i
(An-
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“The best of people are those most beneficial to
i
people.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tabarani.)
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is
i
responsible for his flock.”
i
(Agreed upon.)
Imam Ibn ’Ashur (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The
greatest purpose of the Shari’ah is the preservation of the order
of the nation.” (See:
Maqasid Al-Shari’ah Al-Islamiyyah
i
by Ibn
’Ashur.) This statement affirms the importance of achieving
social stability and order in the life of the nation.
Society in Islam, then, is not a collection of isolated
individuals, but a network of mutual solidarity and shared
responsibility.
Chapter 4: Islam in a Changing World
b
Among the characteristics of Islam is that it unites the fixity of
its principles with the flexibility of its means. Allah, the
Exalted, says:
“So remain upright as you have been commanded”
i
The Prophet ﷺ said to the Companions:
“You are more
i
knowledgeable in the affairs of your worldly life.”
i
(Reported by
Muslim.)
Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“The Shari’ah is justice entire, mercy entire, and wisdom
entire.” (See:
I’lam Al-Muwaqqi’in ’an Rabb Al-’Alamin
i
by
Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim.) This statement affirms the importance
of understanding the Shari’ah in realizing the public interest
and justice.
Imam Al-Shatibi (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him)
said: “The purposes are fixed, while the means change with
the changing of the times.” (See:
Al-Muwafaqat fi Usul Al-
i
Shari’ah
i
by Imam Al-Shatibi.) This means: the fundamental
purposes of the Shari’ah are fixed, but the means of realizing
them change according to time and circumstance, and this
statement affirms the importance of accounting for changing
conditions, and of adapting the means to realize the purposes
of the Shari’ah.
Islam, then, does not clash with the age, nor dissolve within
it, but directs it by the highest values.
Conclusion of Part 9
b
Islam is a comprehensive vision, a system for living, and a
civilizational project. When Islam is understood in its entirety,
the illusory conflict with the age dissolves, religiosity turns
into a force of construction, and religion recovers its role in
guiding the human being.
From this understanding we move to the final question: how
do we transform this awareness into practical action?
Part 10: From Understanding to Action
b
Introduction to Part 10:
b
the crisis of the nation today does not
lie in a shortage of texts, nor in the obscurity of revelation, nor
in the scarcity of exhortation, but in the gap between what we
know and what we live.
How many a Muslim memorizes the verses of the Qur’an,
repeats the Prophetic hadiths, and performs the religious rites,
and yet this is never reflected in his character, his dealings, or
his decisions.
For this reason, the transition from understanding to action is
the true challenge of contemporary religiosity, and it is the true
measure of the fruit of faith. This Part contains four chapters
and a conclusion.
Chapter 1: A Crisis of Application, Not a Crisis of Text
b
Revelation is complete, guidance is clear, but the disorder lies
in its implementation. Allah, the Exalted, says:
“This day I
i
have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon
i
you and have approved for you Islam as religion”
i
(Al-Ma’idah 5:3).
Allah, the Exalted, also says:
“[This is] a blessed Book which We
i

The path to Allah is neither obscure, nor complicated, nor
confined to an elite few apart from the rest of humanity, that

sincere hearts, possessed of conscious minds and firm deeds,

This religion has taught us that nearness to Allah is not
measured by an abundance of slogans, nor by the sharpness of
one’s rhetoric, nor by the inflation of disagreements, but is
measured by a precise scale: the sincerity of faith, the
soundness of deed, and benefit brought to Allah’s creation.

nor by deeds devoid of awareness.
This book has attempted to reorder our relationship with

clouded our understanding, and what has accumulated, in
practice, of rigidity or hollowness, affirming that:

it is a doctrinal or verbal concept.
2. The acts of worship are instruments for building a

4. Zakat is an economy of mercy, not merely the payment

5. Fasting is a school of the will, not merely the
abandonment of food, drink, and appetite.
6. Hajj is a declaration of nationhood, not a commercial

General Summary of the Book
b
The Balanced Scale: A Contemporary Reading of Islam, and a
i
Renewal of Religion’s Effect on Life
i
This book proceeds from a central premise: that the crisis of
Muslims today is not a crisis of religion, but a crisis of
understanding and application of it, for the text has not
changed, and revelation remains preserved, but reality has
been transformed, and the variables of reality have multiplied.
Part 1, Introduction to the Book: An Age of
b
Transformations.
b
This Part affirms that understanding
religion in an age of transformation requires a renewal of
understanding, not a renewal of religion itself, and confirms
that stagnation freezes religion within the moulds of its own
history, while dissolution empties it of the essence of its
message; and it presents Islam as the religion of innate human
nature and reason together, balancing between fixity and
movement, between discipline and flexibility.
Part 2, Monotheism: The Centre of the Whole Structure.
b
The book presents monotheism not as a mere doctrinal, verbal
concept, but as that which liberates the human being from
servitude to creation and makes him a servant of Allah alone;
the two testimonies of faith are not a verbal formula, but a way
of life; and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is not merely a conveyor
of legislation, but the one who connects revelation’s guidance
to practical action in reality.
Part 3, Faith: Between Its Attachment to Knowledge and
b
Its Attachment to Submission.
b
Part 4, Acts of Worship: Between Form and Function.
b
The
book clarifies that acts of worship were legislated to build the
balanced human being, and that measuring their soundness by
their behavioural effect is one of the greatest signs of formal
religiosity, whereas true worship is an inward expression, not
a ritual detached from life.
Part 5, Prayer: The Bond of Life.
b
The book presents prayer
as the balance of one’s daily faith, and a school of discipline
and self-mastery, and the book uncovers that a false sense of
futility is often the cause of a person’s aversion to worship if
the awareness of its wisdom and purpose is lacking.
Part 6, Zakat: An Economy of Mercy.
b
The book
demonstrates that wealth is a trust, not an act of ownership;
that zakat is a tool of justice, addressed to society, not merely
to the individual; and that mutual solidarity is the foundation
for achieving social balance, and the key to civilizational
stability.
Part 7, Fasting: Rebuilding the Human Being.
b
The book
presents fasting as a school for training the will and self-
restraint, and resisting consumerism and appetite, and affirms
that leaving Ramadan without any real change is a warning
sign requiring a review of one’s understanding of the fast’s true
purpose.
Part 8, Hajj: The Nation in a Single Scene.
b
The book
presents Hajj as a rite that unites the nation across time and
space, embodying its unity in its outward appearance, and re-
establishing this unity in the greater purpose, and gathers
civilizational lessons in discipline, equality, and collective
responsibility.
Part 9, Islam: And the System of Contemporary Life.
b
The
book affirms that Islam does not clash with knowledge, nor is
it hostile to reason, but presents a rightly guided,
comprehensive vision that engages with the variables of the
age, uniting between the fixed and the practical.
Part 10, From Understanding to Action.
b
The book concludes
that the true crisis lies not in the text, but in its application, nor
in the Shari’ah, but in the human being, whose understanding
has not been transformed into responsibility, for individual
piety, without a collective consciousness, is not sufficient to
help build reality.
Conclusion.
b
The book concludes that the path to Allah is
neither obscure nor complicated, but requires clarity of
understanding, sincerity of deed, and steadfastness of method,
for Islam was never, in the mind of its Founder, Allah, exalted
is He above such a description, a burden upon life, but has
always been a way to its flourishing and to guiding it, together.
Knowing the Self:
b
The Path to Uprightness
b

b
