Introduction to the Book
b
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
i
All praise is due to Allah, who created us and taught us, who
gave us hearts with which to think and eyes with which to see
and tongues with which to speak good, who deposited within
our souls the secrets of guidance and misguidance, and who
made their purification the path to success and their neglect
the cause of loss.
Everlasting prayers and peace be upon our Prophet
Muhammad, who called for knowledge and righteous action
at every stage of life, and upon his family, his companions,
and all who follow them in righteousness until the Day of
Judgement. To proceed:
The human soul is the arena in which the call of truth
contends with the promptings of desire; it is the site of trial
and the centre from which direction is taken. To the degree
that a person knows their own soul, so too will their awareness
of their path and their steadfastness upon it grow, for there can
be no outward uprightness alongside inward corruption, no
soundness of deed without sincerity, and no firmness upon
truth without struggling against and holding the soul to
account.
It has become common among people to busy themselves with
reforming appearances while neglecting the reform of hearts,
so the balance has been thrown off and conduct has grown
unsettled; claims have multiplied while sincerity has grown
scarce.
From this arises the pressing need to reconsider the self: to
define its true nature, to explain its divisions, to expose its
afflictions, to draw attention to the avenues by which Satan
enters it, and to lay down a practical method for its
purification in the light of revelation, the guidance of the
righteous predecessors, and the experience of those who raise
and educate others.
This book is a modest attempt to show that knowing the self
is not an end, but a means to uprightness; and that purifying it
is not a moral luxury but a religious obligation, through which
the heart lives, conduct is set right, and both the individual
and society are reformed.
We have taken care throughout to combine sound scriptural
grounding, an educational approach, and practical
application, avoiding both tedious length and reductive
brevity.
Dear reader, whether you are young or old, a young man or a
young woman, in middle age or advanced years, know that
life is a journey filled with beautiful things but also filled with
challenges and temptations.
Allah created the human being in the most excellent form,
placing within them strength and weakness, body and spirit,
desire and reason, such that life becomes a journey of testing
and trial. Among the greatest purposes of this journey is that
a person remains upright upon the path of truth, so that they
may succeed in this world and the next.
But how does a person remain upright? And what is the way
to know the correct path in life?
The answer to this question lies in knowing the self,
understanding the stages of life, understanding one’s
surrounding environment, and understanding what draws a
person toward uprightness and what draws them toward sin.
A person who knows themselves, who knows their points of
weakness and strength, and who knows the influence of those
around them, can balance their desires and appetites against
their duty toward Allah and so walks the path of uprightness
with steadiness.
To walk the correct path and please Allah, we need to know
ourselves. On this journey, a person needs to know themselves
to recognize their points of strength and weakness, so that they
may walk the path of uprightness with steadiness.
What is it that makes us upright? And what is it that may draw
us away from truth and uprightness?
This book will accompany you as a friend, guiding you, Allah
willing, to know yourself well:
1. In your childhood, your youth, your middle age, your old
age, and your advanced years.
2. In your home, your village or city or country or the world
entire, amid your brothers and sisters, your friends and
neighbours, and your communities.
3. In the age of technology and modern developments,
material and immaterial alike.
Whoever knows themselves and knows their environment
becomes better able to make sound decisions, to preserve their
religion, and to live with happiness and tranquillity.
This book offers you a simple map for understanding yourself
through the different stages of your life, from childhood to old
age; for distinguishing between the motives of uprightness and
the motives of sin at each stage; for recognizing the influence
of environment, society, custom, and tradition, as well as the
developments of the age; and for following a balanced
approach between the pull of the earth and the pull of the
heaven. It is hoped that this book will serve as a practical guide
for the seeker of uprightness, and a companion for anyone
who wishes to understand themselves and steady their steps in
this life so full of challenges and temptations. It will acquaint
you with:
1. The motives of uprightness and sin at every stage of life.
2. The influence of environment, society, custom, tradition,
and other such factors.
3. How to deal with the developments of the age in a way
that preserves your religion and your character.
Whoever knows themselves and surrounds that knowledge
with awareness can balance their desires against their duty
toward Allah, so that their heart is illuminated with faith and
their deeds bear fruit in righteousness, in this world and the
next.
My reader, read, reflect upon it, and try to apply what is in it
step by step, that your life may become a journey of
uprightness and the joy of Allah’s pleasure upon you.
We ask Allah, Mighty and Sublime, to benefit you through
this book, to make you among those who walk His straight
path, and to make you firm upon it.
Prologue
b
Allah, the Exalted, says:
“And within yourselves, do you not then
i
see?”
i
(Adh-Dhariyat 51:21)
For a person to know their own self is an act of worship, a
form of insight, and a great means to uprightness, for whoever
knows the places of their weakness struggles against them
well, and whoever knows the places of their strength gives
thanks well.
A person cannot achieve true uprightness upon the command
of Allah unless they know themselves: their weakness and
their strength, their needs and their appetites, and what
intensifies within them at one time and weakens at another.
Knowing the self is not an end, but a means toward self-
formation, spiritual struggle, and a sound course toward
Allah. Uprightness is not an occasional matter in a person’s
life, nor conduct that appears at one time and vanishes at
another; it is a lifelong course requiring constant awareness,
insight, and struggle. Among the greatest things that help a
person along this course is that they come to know themselves
with true knowledge. A person carries within them
contradictory impulses: impulses that call them to good and
obedience, and others that pull them toward appetite, desire,
and heedlessness.
A servant cannot govern this inner conflict except by
understanding the nature of their own self, knowing the places
of its weakness and strength, and grasping how its needs and
appetites change across the different stages of life.
Nor does a person live in isolation; they are surrounded by an
environment and a society, with their customs and traditions
and the influences within them, influences that may either
assist uprightness or turn one away from it. And with the
accelerating developments of this age and the changing
patterns of life, the need for this awareness has become more
pressing and necessary.
Hence this book, intended as a simplified educational guide to
help the reader understand themselves through the different
stages of life, to recognize the difference between what draws
one toward uprightness and what draws one toward sin, and
to walk toward Allah with insight and balance. Whoever
knows themselves finds it easier to set themselves right;
whoever knows their path stumbles less; and whoever walks
the path of uprightness with knowledge is made firm and
aided by Allah.
Part 1: The Human Being Between the Pull of the Earth
b
and the Pull of the Heaven
b
Introduction:
b
The human being is a wondrous creation,
possessed of an earthly, dust-born dimension and a spiritual,
heavenly dimension. For this reason, a person is always
caught in an inner struggle: between the call of appetite and
the call of faith, between desire and God-consciousness
(Taqwa), between the pull of the earth and the pull of the
heaven.
The Qur’an summed up this reality in a magnificent verse:
“And [by the soul] and He who proportioned it and inspired it with
i
discernment of its wickedness and its righteousness. He has succeeded
i
who purifies it, and he has failed who instils it [with corruption].”
i
(Ash-Shams 91:7–10). Within every human being, then, are
two opposing forces: one that drives them toward wickedness,
and one that calls them toward righteousness. This Part
contains twelve chapters.
Chapter 1: The Reality of the Struggle Within the Human
b
Being
b
The human being is neither purely angelic nor purely satanic,
but rather a composite being: a body inclined toward the earth,
and a spirit that yearns for the heaven. Allah says:
“And
i
certainly did We create man from an extract of clay”
i
(Al-Mu’minun
23:12) and then says:
“Then We produced him as another
i
creation”
i
(Al-Mu’minun 23:14), a reference to the breathing-in
of the spirit. For this reason, a person lives constantly between
two calls:
1. The call of eat, drink, enjoy, sleep, marry, rest, and wear
fine clothing, as Allah says:
“And eat and drink, but be not
i
excessive”
i
(Al-A’raf 7:31).
2. The call of worship Allah, obey the Messenger, pray, give
in charity from your wealth, fast, be conscious of Allah,
and do good to people, as Allah says:
“So pray to your Lord
i
and sacrifice [to Him alone]”
i
(Al-Kawthar 108:2).
Chapter 2: The Heart Is the Battlefield
b
Allah made the heart the centre of this struggle. The Prophet
ﷺ said:
“Indeed, within the body there is a morsel of flesh: if it is
i
sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is
i
corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.”
i
(Agreed upon). The heart, then,
is the command room, the centre of direction, the source of
decision.
When faith prevails within it, a person is drawn toward the
heaven, answering the call of faith. When appetite prevails
within it, a person is drawn toward the earth, answering the
call of appetite.
Chapter 3: The Pull of the Earth
b
What is meant by the pull of the earth is: appetite, desires, love
of this worldly life. Allah says:
“Beautified for people is the love of
i
that which they desire, of women, children, heaped-up sums of gold
i
and silver, fine branded horses, and cattle and tilled land. That is the
i
enjoyment of worldly life, but Allah has with Him the best return.”
i
(Aal ’Imran 3:14), and He says:
“But you prefer the worldly life”
i
This pull leads a person to incline toward comfort, love
pleasure, dislike obligations, and forget the Hereafter.
Chapter 4: The Pull of the Heaven
b
Opposite this stands another pull: the pull of faith, the pull of
obedience, the pull of values, the pull of the Hereafter. Allah
says:
“But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah”
i
(Al-
Baqarah 2:165), and He says:
“He has certainly succeeded who
i
purifies it”
i
(Ash-Shams 91:9).
This pull raises a person: from clay to the loftiest heights, from
appetite to God-consciousness, from heedlessness to spiritual
wakefulness.
Chapter 5: The True Measure of Distinction Between
b
People
b
Superiority is not measured by wealth, nor by status, nor by
physical strength, but by one’s capacity to resist the pull of the
earth and answer the call of the heaven. Allah says:
“Indeed,
i
the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you”
i
(Al-Hujurat 49:13), and the Prophet ﷺ said:
“The true struggler
i
(mujahid) is the one who strives against his own self in obedience to
i
Allah, Mighty and Sublime.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tirmidhi).
The true hero, then, is not the one who triumphs over other
people or over jinn, but the one who triumphs over the desires
of his own soul.
Chapter 6: The Nature of Human Trial
b
Allah made this struggle a test for the human being. He says:
“[He] who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best
i
indeed”
i
(Al-Mulk 67:2), and He also says:
“Indeed, We guided
i
him to the way, be he grateful or ungrateful”
i
(Al-Insan 76:3). A
person is thus given the choice between two paths: the path of
appetite, and the path of uprightness.
Chapter 7: Means of Strengthening the Pull of the Heaven
b
For a person to triumph over their own self, they need several
means, among them:
1. Sincere faith, Allah says:
“The believers are only those who,
i
when Allah is mentioned, their hearts become fearful”
i
(Al-
Anfal 8:2).
2. Continuous worship, Allah says:
“And worship your Lord

Chapter 10: The Practical Reality of This Struggle
b
Every person feels this struggle daily, whether they are
conscious of it, and it comes to them:
1. When the caller to prayer says at dawn, “Prayer is better
than sleep”, between sleep and prayer.
2. When earning a livelihood, between being content with
the lawful alone or taking the unlawful.
3. When feeling anger, between forgiving for Allah’s sake or
seeking revenge for oneself.
4. During trial and temptation, between following desire or
following the call of God-consciousness.
Chapter 11: The Meaning of the Two Pulls
b
Allah created the human being and placed within them two
opposing dimensions: the pull of the heaven and the pull of
the earth.
1. The pull of the earth: the bodily needs of food, drink,
sleep, and intimacy, and the appetites that follow from
them.
2. The pull of the heaven: the needs of the spirit, faith,
obedience, a living conscience, and longing for Allah and
the Hereafter.
3. The whole of human need is a constant movement
between these two pulls, and no one is free of it.
Chapter 12: Uprightness Is the Fruit of Balance
b
Uprightness does not mean abolishing the body, nor
neglecting the spirit; it means governing the pull of the earth

through life as a servant of Allah, not a servant of their own
appetites.
Comprehensive Summary of Part 1
b
The human being is a creature living between two worlds: the
body pulling toward the earth, and the spirit pulling toward
the heaven. True happiness lies in the pull of the heaven
prevailing over the pull of the earth.

b
1. Whoever is overcome by the pull of the heaven rises,
finds tranquillity, attains happiness, and is saved.

An Educational Note
b
Whatever a person’s circumstances, their stage of life, their
level of knowledge, the influence of their environment, their
health or illness, they live between:

pleasure.
2. The motives of uprightness: faith, obedience, fear of
Allah, hope in the Hereafter.
No stage of a person’s life is free from this struggle, but the
proportions of these motives differ from one stage to another,

b

b

b

After the stage of youth, human life
passes through two great turning points:
1. The stage of middle age (kuhulah): the stage of
intellectual maturity and life-balance.
2. The stage of old age (shaykhukhah): the stage of gradual
weakening and return to one’s origin.

i
grey hair”

weakness of childhood, the strength of youth, the balance of
middle age, and the weakness of old age.
Chapter 1: Middle Age, the Stage of Balance and Maturity
b
1. The nature of this stage: in middle age, a person has
matured intellectually, settled psychologically, calmed
their impulses, and gained increased experience of life. It
is the stage of complete reasoning, emotional balance,
and sound judgement. Allah says:
“And when he attained
i
his full strength and was mature, we bestowed upon him
i
judgement and knowledge”
i
(Al-Qasas 28:14), evidence that
middle age is a time of wisdom, of decision-making, and
of bearing great responsibilities.
2. The trials of middle age: although this stage is one of
balance, it carries its own trials, among them: the trial of
wealth, the trial of position, the trial of family and
children, and the trial of firmness upon principle. Allah
says:
“And We test you with evil and with good as trial”
i
(Al-
Anbiya 21:35).
3. Responsibility at this stage: a person now typically
becomes a father, a spouse, a leader, an educator. For this
reason, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Each of you is a shepherd, and
i
each of you is responsible for his flock.”
i
(Reported by Al-
Bukhari.) The trial here is one of trust and responsibility
more than one of desire or impulsiveness.
4. The balance required in middle age: what is required of a
person at this stage is moderation, wisdom, combining
this world and the next, and being a good example for
those who follow. Allah says:
“And thus We have made you
i
a just, balanced community”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:143).
Chapter 2: Old Age, the Stage of Gradual Weakening
b
The reality of this stage: after strength and balance comes
Allah’s inevitable decree. Allah says:
“And among you is he who
i
is returned to the most decrepit age”
i
(An-Nahl 16:70).
1. Old age is a stage of bodily weakness, diminished
physical energy, declining capacity, and increased need
for others.
2. The wisdom of this stage: among the greatest wisdoms in
old age are reminding a person of the truth of their
weakness, severing attachment to this world, preparing to
meet Allah, and returning a person to their original state.
Allah says:
“And whoever We grant long life, we reverse in
i
creation”
i
3. The trials of old age: the trials of this stage differ from all
that came before: the trial of illness, the trial of incapacity,
the trial of loneliness, the trial of needing others, and the
trial of patience amid pain. For this reason, the Prophet
ﷺ used to supplicate:
“O Allah, I seek refuge in You from
i
decrepit old age.”
i
(Reported by Al-Bukhari in his Sahih.)
4. The greatest virtue of this stage: patience with bodily
pain, contentment with Allah’s decree, and offering
counsel and guidance to children and grandchildren.
5. The most important worship in old age is contentment
with the decree of Allah, patience with weakness,
abundant remembrance of Allah, invoking blessings
upon the Prophet, seeking forgiveness, and supplication.
The Prophet ﷺ said:

i
believer, all his affairs are good for him, and this is for only the

him.”

(Al-Ma’arij 70:5).

b
Age and Old Age

Among the educational errors is the belief that worship

i
seedling in his hand, let him plant it.”

i

i
elders.”

b
That strength is temporary; that this world is ever-changing;
that wisdom ripens with time; and that preparation for the
Hereafter is the work of an entire lifetime.
Summary of Part 3
b
Middle age is the stage of balance, maturity, and giving. Old
age is the stage of weakness, and of turning toward Allah for
a good ending, and toward people for assistance. Each stage
has its own duties and trials. The wise person is the one who
knows what is required of them at each stage.

Whoever understands Allah’s established way in middle age

Incapacity and advanced old age, the stage in which desire

i
decrepit age”

(An-Nahl 16:70).

i

Among the greatest of Allah’s established ways in His creation

hair”

(Ar-Rum 30:54). This stage is the final station of worldly

Chapter 1: The Nature of This Stage
b
The stage of incapacity and advanced old age is marked by
several characteristics: bodily weakness, diminished activity,
fading desire, increased experience, clarity of vision, and
soundness of judgement.
It is a stage in which the dominion of the body weakens while
the dominion of the intellect grows strong. The meaning of
“weak desire, strong argument”:
1. In youth, desire is strong, emotion prevails, and wisdom
is limited.
2. In old age, desire quiets, cravings subside, experience
comes to the fore, and a person becomes more capable of
understanding and judgement. Hence it was said: “The
opinion of the elder is better than the exploits of the
young.”
Chapter 2: The Qur’anic Evidence for This Reality
b
Allah says:
“And among you is he who is returned to the most
i
decrepit age so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing”
i
(An-Nahl
16:70). This verse indicates that old age weakens the body and
may weaken memory, but it generally strengthens insight and
experience before one reaches the most decrepit stage of all.
Allah also relates the words of Zechariah:
“And old age has
i
reached me”
i
(Aal ’Imran 3:40), old age, then, is mentioned in
the Qur’an in connection with wisdom and dignity.
Chapter 3: Advanced Old Age, a School of Wisdom
b
At this stage a person becomes more forbearing, less
impulsive, more capable of self-restraint, and further from
haste, for which reason the Arabs used to say: “Sound
judgement lies with those advanced in years.”
Evidence from the Sunnah: the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Blessing
i
accompanies your elders.”
i
(Reported by Ibn Hibban.) This hadith
shows that the elderly are generally people of experience,
sound opinion, and deserve respect and esteem. The Prophet
ﷺ also said:
“He is not of us who does not honour our elders.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tirmidhi.)
Chapter 4: The Changing Nature of Trial at This Stage
b
In youth, trial generally comes through desires, wealth, status,
and the struggle against one’s own inclinations.
In old age, trial comes through patience with weakness,
bearing illness, contentment with the decree, and dependence
upon others.
For this reason, the Prophet ﷺ used to supplicate:
“O Allah, I
i
seek refuge in You from worry and grief, and I seek refuge in You from
i
incapacity and laziness.”
i
(Reported by Al-Bukhari and Muslim.)
Incapacity, then, is among the greatest trials of this stage.

b
Life
b
Among Allah’s wisdoms is that the more a person’s years
advance, the more their understanding of life deepens, the
more they perceive the consequences of things, the more they
learn from their errors, and the more insightful they become.

“But above every possessor of knowledge is one more
i
knowing”
i
(Yusuf 12:76). Old age, then, is not merely a stage of
decline, but a stage of intellectual and spiritual maturity.

b

remembrance of Allah, passing on experience to the younger
generations, patience with what Allah has decreed, preparing
to meet Allah, praying for good for the coming generations,
and holding a good opinion of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“When Allah intends good for His servant, He hastens his

punishment in this world.”

Chapter 7: Society’s Duty Toward the Elderly
b
Islam accords the elderly an exalted standing: respect, care,
esteem, and kindness. Allah says:
“And your Lord has decreed
i
that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment.
i
Whether one or both reach old age with you, do not say to them a
i
word of disrespect, and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble
i
word.”
i
(Al-Isra’ 17:23). This verse is a complete constitution
for dealing with the elderly.
Chapter 8: The Balance of This Stage Between Intellect and
b
Spirit
b
When desire weakens, the opportunity grows greater for:
devoting oneself to worship, correcting one’s course,
increasing repentance, and taking stock of oneself. Allah says:
“And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty
i
[death]”
i
(Al-Hijr 15:99).
Chapter 9: Lessons Drawn from This Stage
b
Among the most important lessons at this stage: that desire is
fleeting; that strength is closer to passing away; that wisdom
is the fruit of experience; that a person’s worth lies not in their
strength but in their insight; and that the best provision in old
age is righteous deed.
Summary of Part 4
b
Advanced old age is a stage of physical weakness, yet one of
intellectual and spiritual strength, a stage in which the
dominion of desire recedes, and the voice of wisdom rises, and
in which a person draws closer to the meeting with their Lord.
Conclusion
b
The wise person is the one who understands the message of
this stage: thanking Allah for what has passed, being patient
with what remains, and preparing for the Hereafter in the best
possible way, as Allah says:
“The Day when there will not benefit
i
[anyone] wealth or children, but only one who comes to Allah with a
i
sound heart”
i
(Ash-Shu’ara 26:88–89).
Educational estimate of proportions:
b
1. Motives toward sin
at this stage are very, very, very weak (approximately 10–
20%). 2. Motives toward uprightness at this stage are very,
very strong (approximately 80–90%).
For this reason, moral transgression at this stage is more
severely detested in the sight of Allah, since it occurs despite
weak desire, the nearness of departure, and the clarity of truth.
Part 5: The Just Educational Balance Between the Stages
b
of Life
b
Introduction to this Part:
b
Allah says:
“[He] who created death
i
and life to test you as to which of you is best indeed”
i
(Al-Mulk 67:2).
This noble verse establishes the great principle of Islamic
education: that human life is a sequence of stages, each with
its own balance and its own appropriate test, and that what is
required of the servant at every stage is to be
best
b
indeed, not
merely
most
b
indeed.
Chapter 1: The Meaning of the Just Educational Balance
b
What is meant by the just educational balance is that an
educator, or a person dealing with their own self, engage
according to the stages of life, one’s capacities, and one’s
circumstances, without excess or negligence, and without
burdening oneself or others beyond what they can bear.
It is not wise to demand of a child what is demanded of a
youth, nor to treat a beginner in the pursuit of knowledge as
one treats a scholar, nor to measure a newly repentant person
by the standards of the earliest generations of Islam. This is
among the deep understanding (Fiqh) of religion and
education.
Qur’anic evidence for attending to the different stages: Allah
says:
“Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its
i
capacity”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:286), and He also says:
“And Allah
i
brought you out from the wombs of your mothers not knowing a
i
thing”
i
(An-Nahl 16:78).
These verses indicate that a person progresses gradually in
knowledge, gradually in capacity, and gradually in the
obligations placed upon them. From this it follows that
teaching and upbringing must proceed through balanced
stages.
Chapter 2: The Meaning of “Best indeed,” Not “Most
b
indeed”
b
The verse did not say, “most of you indeed,” but rather:
“which
i
of you is best indeed.”
i
Al-Fudayl ibn ’Iyad (may Allah have mercy on him) explained
this: “Best indeed means most sincere and most correct, for a
deed that is sincere but not correct is not accepted, and a deed
that is correct but not sincere is not accepted.” (See
Siyar A’lam
i
Al-Nubala’
i
by Al-Dhahabi, and
Hilyat Al-Awliya’
i
by Abu
Nu’aym Al-Asbahani.)
This shows that the balance is not the quantity of deeds, but
rather: sound understanding, sincerity of intention,
conformity with the Sunnah, and attentiveness to one’s stage
and capacity.
Chapter 3: The True Meaning of Asceticism (Zuhd) Within
b
This Balance
b
Imam Sufyan Al-Thawri (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“The ascetic is not the one who abandons this world, but the
one who knows it’s true worth.” (See
Siyar A’lam Al-Nubala’
i
by Al-Dhahabi, and
Hilyat Al-Awliya’
i
by Abu Nu’aym Al-
Asbahani.)
This is a tremendous principle in education, for balanced
upbringing does not call for hatred of this world,
abandonment of work, or neglect of cultivating the earth.
Rather, it calls for placing this world in its proper position, as
a means, not an end.
Qur’anic evidence for this understanding: Allah says:
“But
i
seek, through that which Allah has given you, the home of the
i
Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world”
i
(Al-Qasas
28:77), a clear balance between religion and this world, spirit
and body, worship and work.
It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said:
“Indeed, your Lord
i
has a right over you, your own self has a right over you, and your
i
family has a right over you, so give each due its right.”
i
(Reported by
Al-Bukhari.) This hadith is the golden rule of the educational
balance: no monasticism in Islam, and no immersion in
worldliness, but rather balance and justice between rights and
duties.
Chapter 4: Gradualism in Prophetic Education
b
The Prophet ﷺ raised the Companions in stages: beginning
with faith before rulings, beginning with creed before its
branches, beginning with the purification of hearts before
multiplying obligations.
’A’ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said:
“What was first
i
revealed of it were short chapters mentioning Paradise and the Fire,
i
until when people had turned to Islam, [verses on] the lawful and
i
unlawful were revealed.”
i
(Reported by Al-Bukhari.) This is
practical evidence for the graduated educational balance.
Chapter 5: Statements of the Scholars on Attending to the
b
Stages of Life
b
Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Whoever knows the stages of the path but does not attend to
people’s different ranks corrupts more than he sets right.” (See
Ibn Al-Qayyim’s books:
Madarij Al-Salikin
i
and
Al-Fawa’id
i
This statement shows that whoever knows the path to Allah
but fails to attend to people’s varying levels within religion
may end up doing more harm than good.
Imam Al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The
obligations of the Shari’ah are built upon ease, the removal of
hardship, and attentiveness to capacity.” (See Al-Shatibi’s
books:
Al-Muwafaqat fi Usul Al-Shari’ah
i
and
Al-I’tisam
i
This statement shows that Islamic law considers ease and the
removal of hardship for people and considers a person’s ability
and capacity.
Ibn Mas’ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: “You are
in a time in which its jurists are many and its orators are few,
and a time will come in which its jurists are few and its orators
are many.” (Reported by Al-Darimi in his Sunan, and Ibn Abi
Shaybah in
Al-Musannaf
i
This statement shows that in the time of the Companions,
jurists were many and orators were few, whereas in our own
time, jurists will grow scarce and orators will multiply.
This points to the necessity of patient, gradual upbringing;
understanding before action; and foundation-building before
the imposition of obligations.
Chapter 6: Practical Applications of the Educational
b
Balance
b
Just balance requires that we consider, in upbringing,
guidance, teaching, and da’wah:
1. The stages of life: teach and endear religion to the child;
guide and steady the youth; consolidate and draw upon
experience with the elder.
2. The stages of religious commitment: gentleness with the
beginner; guidance for the intermediate; refinement for
the advanced.
3. The variation in capacities: people are not equal in
memorization, nor in understanding, nor in ambition.
Allah says:
“They are [varying] degrees in the sight of Allah”
i
(Aal ’Imran 3:163).
Summary of Part 5
b
The just educational balance rests upon these foundations:
attending to the stages of life, gradualism in obligation,
combining this world and the Hereafter, caring for quality
before quantity, and wisdom and gentleness rather than
harshness and severity.
Conclusion
b
Whoever understands this balance raises themselves correctly,
raises their children in a balanced way, and calls to Allah with
insight, as Allah says:
“Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom
i
and good instruction”
i
Part 6: The Human Being Living Between Two Opposing
b
Sides
b
A human being lives between an angelic side and a bestial
side: a spiritual side that raises them to the ascents of
perfection, and a bodily side that may cast them down to the
depths of decline. If a person elevates their spirit and governs
their body by the light of revelation, they approach the state of
the angels in purity and uprightness; and if they surrender to
their desires, giving free rein to the body without measure,
they descend until they resemble the animal in their
subjugation to instinct and its dominance over them.
A human being lives between resembling the angels and
resembling the animals, between the pull of the heaven and
the pull of the earth. Allah says:
“We have certainly created man
i
in the best of stature; then We return him to the lowest of the low”
i
Chapter One
b
A human being is not a creature of fixed direction, nor a being
of a single dimension, but a composite existence living in a
state of constant tension between two opposing forces: one
that raises them to the heights of perfection, and one that pulls
them down to the depths of decline.
Hence a person stands, throughout their whole life, at a
crossroads, never able to escape the choice between the two
paths.
Chapter 2: The Human Being Between the Potential for
b
Ascent and the Potential for Fall
b
Allah created the human being in the best of forms: a mind
that discerns, a heart that reasons, and a spirit that reaches
beyond the material. Yet this excellence in creation is not a
final guarantee of loftiness, it is a potential, an open project,
that may either be completed or aborted.
If a person answers the call of their spirit, connects with the
unseen, and submits their reins to revelation, they come to
resemble the angels, not in their created form, but in purity of
direction, loftiness of purpose, mastery over desire, and
precedence given to obedience.
But if a person immerses themselves in their desires, unleashes
their instincts without measure, and surrenders to the pull of
the earth, they come to resemble the animal, not in outward
form, but in living by pure instinct, submitting to pleasure, and
worshipping self-interest.
Chapter 3: The Pull of the Heaven and the Pull of the Earth
b
Uprightness, in its true reality, is not a separation from the
earth, nor a suspension of instinct, but rather the management
of balance under the authority of heaven:
1. The pull of the heaven draws a person toward: meaning,
values, purpose, and conscious servitude to Allah.
2. The pull of the earth draws them toward: pleasure,
possession, dominance, and immediate gratification.
A person is not blamed for the presence of both pulls within
them; rather, they are held accountable for which one they
favour: which takes the lead, spirit or appetite? values or
instincts?
Chapter 4: Resembling the Angels, When Heaven Takes the
b
Lead
b
A person draws near to the angels when they make revelation
the standard of their understanding, make the Hereafter the
criterion of their decisions, and make the purification of the
self the purpose of their life.
The description “angelic” here is a description of conduct, not
of created nature, it is discipline, loftiness, and uprightness
within a world filled with temptations.
Hence faith is not merely an idea, but a supreme force of
attraction, redirecting a person whenever they are about to
fall.
Chapter 5: Resembling the Animal, When the Earth Takes
b
the Lead
b
When values are stripped from life, revelation is sidelined, and
a person is reduced to their body alone, they lose their
compass and descend from their humanity without even
realizing it.
This fall to the lowest of the low does not happen suddenly; it
begins with justifying desire, normalizing sin, prioritizing
expedience over principle, and disabling conscience in the
name of “realism”, until a person becomes a captive of that
which they were created to govern, rather than something
governed by it.
Chapter 6: Uprightness, the Path of Salvation Between the
b
Two Extremes
b
Uprightness is not an infallible ideal, but a constant movement
of correction, a repeated return to heaven whenever the earth
pulls us away.
For this reason, the path of uprightness consists of knowledge
of the self, awareness of the inner struggle, nourishment of the
spirit, struggle against desire, and constant connection to
Allah.
Allah says:
“Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous
i
deeds…”
i
(Al-Buruj 85:11), faith preserves the direction, and
righteous deed keeps the course steady.
Conclusion to Part 6
b
A person is not defined by the instincts they possess, for these
they share with the animal, nor are they measured merely by
their intellect, for intellect too may be turned to evil. Rather,
they are measured by their direction: toward what do they
tend, and by which pull do they live?
Whoever lives attached to heaven, walking by its light, is in
the best of stature; and whoever severs their connection to it,
surrendering to the earth alone, is returned to the lowest of the
low.
Part 7: Uprightness Amid Environment and Society Across
b
the Stages of Life
b
Introduction to Part 7:
b
A human being does not live alone,
but within a family, a society, an environment, customs, and
traditions. For this reason, true uprightness is never the
uprightness of an isolated individual, but an uprightness lived
within a reality full of influences and challenges. Allah says:
“To each of you We have prescribed a law and a method”
i
(Al-
Ma’idah 5:48).
The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is
i
responsible for his flock”
i
(Agreed upon). These two texts lay the
foundation of this Part: every stage has its own suitable
approaches, and every person carries a responsibility toward
their environment and society, with the level of uprightness
varying according to the stage of life.
The meaning of uprightness amid environment:
b
uprightness
is not merely individual worship, but rather: steadfastness in
religion, commitment to truth, good conduct toward people,
and the capacity to remain firm despite external influences.
Allah says:
“So remain upright as you have been commanded, and
i
[with you] those who have turned back [to Allah]”
i
He did not say “remain upright alone,” but “and those who
have turned back with you”, a reference to the collective,
societal nature of uprightness.
The meaning of Allah’s words,
“To each of you We have
i
prescribed a law and a method”
i
(Al-Ma’idah 5:48): this verse
indicates that people differ in their environments, differ in
their stages of life, and differ in their capacities, yet what is
required of all is commitment to Allah’s law, with due
attention to their reality, their time, and their society.
Uprightness in a village, then, is not the same as uprightness
in a city, and uprightness in childhood is not the same as
uprightness in youth, middle age, old age, or advanced years.
A person’s responsibility toward their environment:
b
the
Prophet ﷺ said:
“Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is
i
responsible for his flock”
i
(Agreed upon). This hadith is a great
foundation for understanding societal uprightness: the father
is a shepherd in his household, the mother a shepherd in her
family, the teacher a shepherd over his class and students, the
imam a shepherd in his mosque, the young person a shepherd
over their surroundings, the ruler a shepherd over their region,
and the head of state a shepherd over the nation. Uprightness,
then, is not merely saving oneself, but saving those around
oneself as well.
Statements of the scholars on societal uprightness:
b
Imam Al-
Nawawi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “Uprightness
is the sustained obedience of Allah, outwardly and inwardly,
in every state.” (See:
Sharh Sahih Muslim
i
by Al-Nawawi, and
his
Riyad Al-Salihin
i
This statement shows that uprightness means commitment to
obeying Allah, outwardly and inwardly, in all circumstances.
Shaykh Al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on
him) said: “The greatest honour is sustained uprightness.”
(See his books:
Majmu’ Al-Fatawa
i
and
Al-Istiqamah
i
This statement shows that the greatest thing a person can
attain is sustained uprightness upon the path of Allah.
Al-Hasan Al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Faith is not [merely] wishful thinking, nor outward
adornment, but what settles firmly in the heart and is
confirmed by deed.” (See:
Siyar A’lam Al-Nubala’
i
by Al-
Dhahabi, and
Hilyat Al-Awliya’
i
by Abu Nu’aym Al-Asbahani.)
This statement shows that faith is not mere words or wishful
thinking, but what becomes firm in the heart and is confirmed
by action.
These statements together show that uprightness is not
slogans, but practical steadfastness within society.
Practical expressions of uprightness in society:
b
uprightness
manifests in honesty in dealings, trustworthiness in
employment, justice within the family, good neighbourliness,
and counselling people toward good. Allah says:
“And speak to
i
people good [words]”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:83).
Contemporary challenges to uprightness:
b
today a person
faces: the weakening influence of media, the influence of
social media platforms, bad companionship, and many
temptations, yet the principle remains:
“And those who strive for
i
Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways”
i
(Al-’Ankabut 29:69).
Uprightness across the stages of life takes different forms
according to each stage:
Chapter 1: Childhood, the Stage of Reception and
b
Formation
b
In childhood, a person absorbs their environment without full
awareness; their earliest habits are formed by the home and
surroundings, and their capacity to distinguish right from
wrong is still limited.
For this reason, the child is not required to be perfect but is
raised upon the foundations of uprightness: honesty,
trustworthiness, love of prayer, and respect for elders. The
Prophet ﷺ said:
“Command your children to pray when they reach
i
seven, and discipline them for it when they reach ten.”
i
(Reported by
Imam Ahmad in his Musnad.)
A child’s uprightness begins, then, with the home, the school,
and good example. Allah says:
“O you who have believed, protect
i
yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and
i
stones”
i
(At-Tahrim 66:6).
The influence of environment:
b
the family is the first and
strongest environment for a person, and habits are instilled at
this stage before they are ever discussed or debated.
Educational guidance:
b
protecting the child from corrupt
environments, instilling values through example rather than
words, and connecting the child to worship through love, not
compulsion. Allah says:
“And Allah brought you out from the
i
wombs of your mothers not knowing a thing”
i
(An-Nahl 16:78).
Chapter 2: Youth, the Stage of Influence and Choice
b
In the stage of youth, the most perilous of all stages, the need
for belonging intensifies, desires multiply, influences multiply,
the effect of companionship grows immense, social and
intellectual temptations abound, and the pressure of friends
and environment intensifies. For this reason, the greatest
model here remains:
“…and a young man who grew up in the
i
worship of Allah…”
i
(Agreed upon).
Guidance for the young toward uprightness: Allah says:
“And
i
do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of Allah”
i
(Sad 38:26), and the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Guard Allah and He will
i
guard you.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tirmidhi.)
Uprightness in youth, then, comes through choosing righteous
companionship, remaining firm upon prayer, keeping
distance from harmful environments, continuing to seek
knowledge, and channelling one’s energies toward what
pleases Allah.
The influence of environment:
b
friends are more dangerous
than place itself; media shapes convictions; a weakened
society influences decisions. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“A person
i
follows the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look closely at
i
whom he befriends.”
i
(Reported by Abu Dawud Al-Tayalisi in
his Musnad.)
Educational guidance:
b
choosing companionship well;
learning to say “no” to a corrupting environment; being aware
of contemporary developments without being swept along by
them.
A contemporary example:
b
a young man who maintains his
prayers at the mosque and attends circles of knowledge despite
the mockery of his peers, remaining steadfast without cutting
himself off from society.
Chapter 3: Middle Age, the Stage of Influence and
b
Responsibility
b
At this stage, a person becomes more aware, less impulsive,
and more capable of discernment. They become a father, a
spouse, a leader, an example, and so their uprightness lies in:
justice, trustworthiness, raising their children, and reforming
their society. Allah says:
“Indeed, Allah orders justice and good
i
conduct”
i
(An-Nahl 16:90), and Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may
Allah have mercy on him) said: “The uprightness of the elder
is not for himself alone, but a guidance for those who come
after him.” (See Ibn Al-Qayyim’s books:
Madarij Al-Salikin
i
and
Al-Fawa’id
i
This statement shows that the uprightness of a person
advanced in years benefits not only themselves but also serves
as guidance and a model for those who come after.
The influence of environment:
b
a person becomes one who
influences, not merely one who is influenced, and their actions
may be taken as an example. Allah says:
“And We made from
i
among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were
i
patient”
i
(As-Sajdah 32:24).
Educational guidance:
b
reforming one’s environment rather
than fleeing it; raising children with awareness rather than
isolation; guiding social customs rather than adopting them
wholesale.
A contemporary example:
b
regulating the use of technology
within one’s household, to create a wholesome environment
amid an open world.
Chapter 4: Old Age, the Stage of Wisdom and Witness
b
In old age, desires diminish, vision grows clear, and the weight
of one’s words increases. Uprightness here lies in: patience,
abundant remembrance, a good ending, and passing on
experience to the generations. Allah says:
“And worship your
i
Lord until there comes to you the certainty [death]”
i
(Al-Hijr 15:99),
and the Prophet ﷺ said:
“The best of people is he whose life is long
i
and whose deeds are good.”
i
(Reported by Al-Tirmidhi.)
The influence of environment on uprightness:
b
an
environment may be righteous, assisting one toward good, or
corrupt, exerting pressure upon a person. Allah says:
“And
i
keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord
i
in the morning and the evening, seeking His face”
i
(Al-Kahf 18:28),
and the Prophet ﷺ said:
“A person follows the religion of his close
i
friend, so let each of you look closely at whom he befriends.”
i
(Reported by Abu Dawud Al-Tayalisi.)
For this reason, the believer needs righteous companionship,
an upright family, a mosque that assists them toward
obedience, a society that reminds them of their duties, and a
circle of knowledge to nourish them with learning.
Uprightness, then, is not merely an individual effort, but an
integrated system.
The influence of environment:
b
people look to the elder as a
point of reference, and their conduct either strengthens or
corrupts. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“He is not of us who does not
i
honour our elders and show mercy to our young.”
i
(Reported by Al-
Tirmidhi in his Sunan, and Imam Ahmad in his Musnad.)
Educational guidance:
b
that the elder be an example, not one
who is lax; that they warn against deviation rather than justify
it; and that they engage with the age through the balance of
wisdom.
A contemporary example:
b
an elder who uses social media for
counsel and reminder, not to spread discord, or to pry into
people’s faults and private matters.
Chapter 5: Incapacity and Advanced Old Age, the Stage of
b
Steadfastness and Final Counsel
b
At this stage, the body weakens, yet moral responsibility
remains, and one’s final word carries great influence. Allah
says:
“And Abraham instructed his sons [to follow this], and [so did]
i
Jacob, [saying], ‘O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this
i
religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims [submitting to
i
Him].’”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:132).
Educational guidance:
b
steadfastness upon one’s values,
correcting misconceptions before departing this life, and
leaving a righteous mark upon one’s surrounding
environment.
Comprehensive Summary
b
Environment changes, but the standard remains one; every
stage has its own manner of uprightness; and whoever
understands the influence of environment across their lifetime
deals with it well.
An Educational Summary
b
People cannot be measured by a single standard; uprightness
cannot be understood without understanding the nature of
one’s stage of life; and the person of greatest reward is the one
who obeys Allah precisely where sin lay closest at hand.
Conclusion
b
Knowing the self-saves a person from arrogance, prevents
them from despair, teaches them where to be strict with
themselves and where to be grateful to Allah, and it is among
the greatest gateways to uprightness.
Summary of Part 7
b
Uprightness amid environment and society means
steadfastness in religion, fulfilling one’s responsibility,
attending to the different stages, reforming oneself and others,
and adapting to reality without compromising one’s
principles.
Conclusion
b
Whoever understands this Part realizes that uprightness is not
a momentary stance, but the project of an entire lifetime,
beginning in childhood and extending to old age, as Allah
says:
“Indeed, those who have said, ‘Our Lord is Allah,’ and then
i
remained upright, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], ‘Do
i
not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of Paradise, which
i
you were promised.’”
i
(Fussilat 41:30).
Summary of the Book
b
The book
Knowing the Self: The Path to Uprightness
i
rests upon a
central idea: that uprightness is not a fleeting behaviour or a
formal commitment, but the fruit of a deep knowledge of the
human self as Allah created it, together with a precise
understanding of the laws governing its purification and its
deviation, and the principles of its reform and correction. A
person cannot walk a truly straight path toward Allah unless
they know themselves: their motives, their appetites, their
fears, their points of weakness and strength, and how they are
affected by environment, society, and trial.
The book proceeds from the Qur’anic and Prophetic
grounding of the concept of the self, showing that it is not a
single, fixed entity, but rather a field of struggle between the
innate disposition (fitrah) that inclines toward truth, the desire
that pulls it toward deviation, and Satan, who adorns and
justifies. From this arise the varying states of the self, the soul
commanding evil, the self-reproaching soul, and the reassured
soul, and a person’s movement between them is tied to the
extent of their self-awareness and their struggle against their
own inclinations.
This book affirms that many manifestations of religious and
behavioural disorder do not stem from any weakness in the
sacred texts or any deficiency in the Shari’ah, but rather from
ignorance of the self and mishandling it. How many a person
has known the religious ruling, yet been unable to apply it,
because they did not understand the nature of their own self,
did not observe the principle of gradualism, and did not
balance their capacity against what was required of them.
From this arises the educational dimension of the book, which
links knowledge to practice, and faith to conduct, in a realistic
connection that addresses the human being as they are, not as
they are imagined in theory.
The book also addresses the interwoven relationship between
heart, mind, self, and body, establishing that uprightness is an
integrated project encompassing both the inward and the
outward together, for the corruption of the inner self is
reflected in the outward, just as the neglect of the outward
affects the inner self. It therefore holds that acts of worship are
not rituals detached from the self, but instruments of
purification and construction, when performed according to
their true function and purpose, not merely their outward
form.
It further sheds light on the influence of environment and
society in shaping the self, showing that a person is affected by
their surroundings in thought, feeling, and conduct, and that
uprightness within a corrupt environment requires heightened
awareness.
Conclusion
b
In closing: knowing the self is not a theoretical science to be
merely discussed, nor a passing instinct to be admired, it is the
beginning of the path to Allah, the foundation of uprightness,
and the standard by which the heart is purified and conduct is
set right. Whoever knows themselves, their attributes and their
needs, their innate disposition and their purposes, perceives
the flaws within themselves before those in their outward
conduct, and strives to correct them with insight, not
heedlessness.
This book has dealt with the true nature of the self and its
divisions, exposed its afflictions and the avenues by which
Satan approaches it, explained the paths of its purification and
struggle against it, and linked the soundness of the inner self
to the uprightness of outward conduct, affirming that deeds
without sincerity are worthless, and knowledge without
purification is a burden. It has also highlighted the role of self-
accounting, vigilance, repentance, and patience in building a
balanced self, one guided by revelation, illuminated by reason,
and elevated by good character.
This effort has been nothing but a sincere call for a person to
return to themselves in self-accounting, to turn toward their
Lord, and to turn away from heedlessness, that their course
through this life may be one of awareness, not imitation, and
of true uprightness, not mere claim. For the reform of the
individual is the foundation of the reform of society, and the
uprightness of the self is the key to happiness in this world and
the next.
We ask Allah, Mighty and Sublime, to make this work
sincerely for His sake, of benefit to whoever reads it, an aid to
knowing the self, and a means leading to the path of
uprightness. He is the One who grants that, and He is fully
capable of it.
O Allah, send prayers, peace, and blessings upon Your
servant, Your Prophet, and Your Messenger, Muhammad ibn
Abdullah, and upon his family and companions, and upon all
who follow them in righteousness until the Day of Judgement.

Introduction to the Book
b
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
i
All praise is due to Allah, who created the human being for
His worship, who legislated for him a sound religion, who
gave him in His Messenger ﷺ the excellent example, and who
prepared for him, among the scholars and guides, those who
direct him to the path of understanding and action. Prayers
and peace be upon our master Muhammad, the teaching
Prophet and the wise educator, and upon his family, his
companions, and all who follow his guidance until the Day of
Judgement. To proceed:
Among the greatest afflictions besetting the Muslim in this age
is a disorder in the balance of spiritual stations within their
religious life. The defect no longer lies in a shortage of texts or
an absence of models, but in the poor ordering of foundations
and means, of ultimate purposes and subordinate matters.
One sees a Muslim in whom one dimension of religiosity has
come to dominate, overwhelming all the others, producing
thereby a deficient understanding and an unsettled conduct,
even where this appears, on its surface, to be devotion and
zeal.
Some people have reduced religion to a bare spiritual feeling,
thereby weakening the meaning of practical servitude. Others
have made belonging to Islam a cultural identity rather than a
religious obligation. Others still have claimed to emulate the
Messenger ﷺ without any awareness of his comprehensive
method. And others have exalted their sheikh or mentor until
they raised him, beyond the bounds of a mere means, to a
station that rivals the text and the [Prophetic] example itself.
All of this represents a disturbance in the balance, not an
absence of love for religion in people’s hearts.
Islam never intended for the Muslim to live these stations in
discord or conflict with one another; rather, it intended them
to be integrated and harmonious, each with its own limit, its
own function, and its own effect in building the human being.
Servitude to Allah is the foundation upon which the life of
faith is built; belonging to Islam is the methodological
framework that organizes this servitude; emulation of the
Messenger ﷺ is the practical form in which this religion is
embodied in reality; and seeking knowledge at the hands of
scholars and educators is the means that safeguards
understanding from deviation and conduct from disorder.
Yet disorder begins the moment a subordinate matter is given
precedence over a foundation, or a means is elevated to the
rank of an ultimate purpose, or emulation is severed from
understanding, or religion is made subordinate to persons
rather than the reverse.
[In summary: giving precedence to secondary matters over
essential ones; elevating means as though they were ends in
themselves; imitation without understanding; and making
religion subordinate to individuals, rather than individuals
subordinate to religion.]
At that point, partial expressions of religiosity turn into causes
of division, and commitment becomes a source of tension
rather than a path to tranquillity and uprightness.
Hence this book, titled
The Balance of Spiritual Stations in the
i
Muslim’s Life: Servitude, Belonging, Emulation, Receiving
i
Knowledge from a Sheikh
i
, is a practical, educational attempt to
recalibrate this balance, and to return each station to its
rightful place, without erasing it or diminishing it, and without
excess or harshness. It does not call for belittling knowledge
or education, nor for marginalizing belonging or emulation;
rather, it calls for a sound understanding that unites rather
than divides and builds rather than demolishes.
The book follows an analytical, educational method, attentive
to the sacred texts, mindful of the overarching purposes of the
Shari’ah, and engaged with reality without capitulating to it,
keeping always in view the building of the balanced Muslim:
one who knows their Lord, understands their religion,
emulates their Prophet, and learns with insight.
In presenting this work, we do not claim comprehensiveness,
nor do we claim perfection; it is a human effort whose aim is
reform and correction. We hope it may serve as a building
block in constructing sound religious awareness, and a step on
the path toward restoring due regard for the balance by which
the lives of individuals are set right, and the nation (ummah)
is healed.
We ask Allah, the Exalted, to make this work sincerely for His
noble sake, of benefit to its reader, an aid to understanding and
action, and to grant us and you sincerity in servitude,
soundness in belonging, correctness in emulation, and
wisdom in seeking knowledge. He is the One who grants that,
and He is fully capable of it.
[A note on the importance of establishing a clear Muslim identity in
i
an age in which the spiritual stations have become confused, one
i
overwhelming another, producing disorder: some have let spiritual
i
sentiment override the Shari’ah and thus neglected it; some have
i
turned Islam into a bare identity devoid of servitude; some have made
i
their sheikh the foundation and the Messenger (cid:0) merely subordinate
i
to him; and some have claimed emulation without knowledge or
i
proper formation. This introduction affirms that this book is an
i
attempt to restore the correct ordering of these stations, not to separate
i
them, but to bind them together in balanced relation.]

Prologue: The Human Being Between Reception and
b
Obligation
b
Themes of the Prologue:
b
the human being is a worshipping
creature before being a “belonging” creature; the difference
between a station and a means; the danger of conflating the
religious stations; Islam’s approach to ordering priorities.
Summary of the Prologue:
b
the Muslim’s life cannot be sound
unless these stations are understood in their true reality, and
unless the limit and function of each station is known.
Part 1: The Muslim Is a Servant of Allah, Mighty and
b
Sublime
b
Servitude is the foundation of every station, for it lays down
the great principle upon which all the stations of faith and
states of conduct are built; it reorders one’s concepts, so that
every noble station arises only from the realization of
servitude to Allah, and every disorder among the stations
traces back, in truth, to a defect in understanding servitude or
a weakness in its realization. This Part contains eight chapters.
Chapter 1: The Meaning of Servitude in the Islamic
b
Conception
b
Servitude (’ubudiyyah) is not merely the performance of rites,
nor is it a state of passive submission; rather, it is perfect love
joined with perfect humility before Allah, together with
perfect obedience, submission, contentment, and surrender.
The true servant is one who loves Allah with the utmost love,
magnifies Him with the utmost reverence, and submits to Him
outwardly and inwardly. Allah says:
“And I did not create the
i
jinn and mankind except to worship Me”
i
(Adh-Dhariyat 51:56).
Servitude, then, is the supreme purpose of creation, and from
it all the [other] stations branch out.
The meaning of comprehensive servitude:
b
servitude in Islam
is not a partial concept confined to the performance of
outward acts of worship, nor a fleeting psychological state, but
rather a comprehensive existential condition that orders the
whole of a person’s life, outward and inward, heart and form,
secret and open. Through this, servitude is realized in its
complete sense. Comprehensive servitude is the surrender of
the heart to Allah in love and reverence, together with the
compliance of the limbs to Him in obedience and submission.
From here, comprehensive servitude divides into two
fundamental sections:
Section One: Servitude Between Love and Compliance
b
Servitude rests upon two great pillars, neither separable from
the other:
Love
b
, which is the spirit of servitude and its beating heart,
there is no servitude without love, and no obedience
without reverence. Allah says:
“But those who believe are
i
stronger in love for Allah”
i
(Al-Baqarah 2:165). Love of
Allah means giving precedence to what Allah wills over
what people will, rejoicing in obeying Him, grieving over
disobeying Him, and yearning to meet Him. Whoever
loves Allah sincerely finds every obligation made easy for
them.
Compliance
b
, which is the fruit of love and the proof of its
sincerity, for not everyone who claims love is sincere in
that claim, until its effect appears in their conduct. Allah
says:
“Say, [O Muhammad], ‘If you should love Allah, then
i
follow me, [so] Allah will love you’”
i
(Aal ’Imran 3:31).
Compliance includes obeying commands, avoiding
prohibitions, submitting to Allah’s rulings, and being
content with His decree. Love without compliance is an
empty claim, and compliance without love is dry and
lifeless; true servitude unites both together.
Section Two: Servitude of the Heart and Servitude of the
b
Limbs
b
Comprehensive servitude is only realized through the union
of two kinds of servitude:
Servitude of the heart
b
, which is the root of all servitude,
from which all deeds spring. It includes the deeds of the
heart, such as sincerity, reliance upon Allah, fear, hope,
love, and turning [in repentance]. If the heart is sound,
the whole body is sound, and if the heart is corrupt, the
whole body is corrupt. Servitude of the heart is the true
measure by which deeds are accepted.
Servitude of the limbs
b
, which is the translation of the
heart’s servitude into tangible practical reality. It includes
prayer, fasting, almsgiving, pilgrimage, dutifulness to
parents, maintaining family ties, and all other acts of
obedience, together with abandoning what is forbidden.
Sincerity of intention does not dispense with the
soundness of the deed, just as the deed avails nothing
without sincere intention.
The integration of the two kinds:
b
servitude of the heart is the
root, and servitude of the limbs is the branch. If the root is
sound, the branch bears fruit; if the root is corrupt, the branch
withers. For this reason, uniting both is a condition for
realizing comprehensive servitude.
Summary of the two sections:
b
comprehensive servitude rests
upon: sincere love, complete compliance, a living heart, and
active limbs. Through this, the Muslim becomes a true servant
of Allah, and servitude carries them along the path of the
[spiritual] stations, rising from one station to the next, until
they reach whatever nearness [to Allah] He has willed for
them to attain.
Summary of the chapter’s meaning:
b
servitude means that
Allah alone is the object of one’s intention, love, obedience,
hope, and fear.
Chapter 2: Why Is Servitude the Root of Every Station?
b
Because the [spiritual] stations are not independent goals, but
rather fruits of a single tree, the tree of servitude. There is no
sound repentance, no sincere devotion, no beautiful patience,
no beneficial asceticism, and no firm reliance upon Allah,
except where its root is sincere servitude to Allah, the Exalted.
Whoever worships Allah for Allah’s sake, Allah opens for
them the doors of the [spiritual] stations; and whoever
worships the stations [themselves] loses both servitude and the
stations together.
The effects of servitude on the self and conduct:
b
servitude is
not an abstract theoretical concept, but a living reality that
bears clear fruits within a person’s inward and outward life, in
their psychology, their conduct, and their outlook on life.
Whenever comprehensive servitude is realized in heart and
limb, blessed fruits appear, among the greatest of which are: a
person’s liberation from servitude to anything other than
Allah, the attainment of inner tranquillity, and the emergence
of a heightened sense of responsibility and discipline. These
effects divide into two main sections:
Section One: Liberating the Human Being from Attachment
b
to Other than Allah
b
The greatest fruit of servitude is that it releases the heart’s
bonds from everything besides Allah, for the human being is
by nature disposed to attachment, if they do not attach
themselves to Allah, they attach themselves to something else:
wealth, status, people, appetites, or position. When a person
realizes servitude to Allah: they are no longer a captive to
people’s opinions, nor fearful of losing this world, nor
attached to what is in the hands of others. Allah says:
“Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured”
i
(Ar-Ra’d 13:28). Among the manifestations of this liberation:
1. Liberation from servitude to desire, a person governs
their appetite rather than being governed by it.
2. Liberation from servitude to created beings, a person no
longer makes their approval the highest standard but
makes Allah’s approval their goal.
3. Liberation from servitude to this world, a person takes
from it only what they need, making it a means, not an
end.
This liberation does not mean abandoning this world but
placing it in its proper position.
Section Two: Tranquillity and Responsibility
b
Sincere servitude produces two inseparable effects within the
human soul:
Tranquillity
b
, because the servant knows that: they have
a Lord who governs their affairs, a God who does not
neglect His servant, and a refuge to which they may turn
in every circumstance. Their soul settles, their heart
grows calm, and turbulent anxiety departs from them.
The servant neither despairs like one without hope, nor
exults like one filled with arrogance, for they see
everything as coming from Allah and returning to Allah.
Responsibility
b
, true servitude does not produce a passive
human being, but rather one who is: aware of their role,
upright in their work, trustworthy in what they are
charged with, because they feel Allah’s watchfulness over
them, in secret and in the open. They act because they are
commanded, they strive because they are accountable,
and they perfect their work because they know Allah sees
them. From this arise the character traits of honesty,
trustworthiness, discipline, and excellence in work.
The relationship between tranquillity and responsibility:
b
tranquillity grants the heart stillness, and responsibility grants
the limbs motion. Through this, the balanced Muslim is
formed: a heart at rest in Allah, and limbs active for Allah’s
sake, and this is the perfection of servitude.
Summary of this chapter:
b
the more a servant realizes
servitude, the more they are liberated from other than Allah,
the more tranquillity fills their heart, and the more committed
their conduct becomes. Servitude thus transforms from a mere
concept into a way of life.
Chapter 3: Servitude and True Freedom
b
Many people imagine that freedom means breaking every
restraint and being liberated from every authority. Yet this
understanding has led humanity into new forms of servitude,
harsher than the old.
Islam, however, establishes a great truth: no human being is
ever without servitude of some kind, the only real question is,
to whom does that servitude belong? For a person is either a
servant of Allah, Mighty and Sublime, or a servant of their
own desire, their appetite, or another created being like
themselves.
Comprehensive servitude, inward and outward:
b
sincere
servitude to Allah, the Exalted, is realized through three
integrated circles:
Servitude of the heart
b
, including sincerity, reliance upon
Allah, fear and hope, love and turning [to Him], for the
heart is the centre of servitude. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Indeed, within the body there is a morsel of flesh: if it is sound,
i
the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is
i
corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.”
i
(Agreed upon).
Servitude of the tongue
b
, including remembrance of
Allah, supplication, recitation, and enjoining good and
forbidding evil.
Servitude of the limbs
b
, including prayer, fasting,
almsgiving, pilgrimage, and all other bodily acts of
obedience, together with abandoning all that is
forbidden. None of these aspects can substitute for
another.
From here it follows that servitude to Allah alone is true
freedom. This chapter divides into two sections:
Section One: The Difference Between Servitude to Allah
b
and Servitude to Created Beings
b
Servitude to Allah
b
rests upon love, justice, and mercy.
The servant, with Allah knows their purpose, feels secure
about their destiny, and finds rest in the justice of their
Lord. Allah says:
“Allah is the ally of those who believe. He
i
brings them out from darknesses into the light”
i
(Al-Baqarah
2:257). Servitude to Allah liberates the heart, purifies the
soul, and sets conduct right, and the more a servant
submits to Allah, the more liberated they become from
everything else.
Servitude to created beings
b
takes many forms, among
them: servitude to desire, servitude to wealth, servitude
to status, servitude to appetite, and servitude to people, a
servitude built upon anxiety, turbulence, fear, and never
being satisfied. The one enslaved to creation chases
without ever arriving, seeks without ever being quenched.
Allah says:
“Have you seen the one who takes as his god his
i
own desire?”
i
(Al-Jathiyah 45:23). This servitude degrades
a person even if they imagine themselves free.
Comparing the two kinds of servitude:
b
servitude to Allah
brings tranquillity, dignity, and uprightness; servitude to
creation brings anxiety, humiliation, and turmoil. Whoever
recognizes this difference chooses the path of servitude to
Allah with clear insight.
Section Two: Servitude Is the Path to Honour, Not
b
Humiliation
b
Some people imagine that servitude is a form of humiliation.
The truth is that humiliation in Islam belongs only to
submission before other than Allah, while humbling oneself
before Allah is honour itself. Allah says:
“And to Allah belongs
i
[all] honour, and to His Messenger, and to the believers”
i
(Al-
Munafiqun 63:8). When the servant submits to Allah, Allah
raises them, honours them, and dignifies them; whereas
whoever is too proud to serve Allah, Allah humbles them
through something else.
Manifestations of the servant’s honour through servitude:
b
firmness upon truth, strength of principle, independence from
the pressure of others, courage in speaking the truth, and self-
respect, all of these are fruits of sincere servitude.
A great Qur’anic equation:
b
whoever humbles themselves for
Allah, He raises them; and whoever grows arrogant, He
lowers them. Servitude, then, is not a fall but an ascent, not
disgrace but elevation.
Summary of Chapter 3:
b
true freedom lies not in breaking
every restraint, but in choosing the correct restraint. Whoever
chooses to be a servant of Allah is liberated from everything
else and attains honour in this world and happiness in the
Hereafter.
Chapter 4: Servitude in States of Ease and Hardship
b
True servitude is not a passing condition, nor a temporary
stance connected to hardship alone; it is a permanent station
that encompasses all the changing circumstances of human
life, in abundance and constraint, in health and illness, in
strength and weakness, in obedience and shortcoming. The
true servant does not turn their heart in a different direction as
circumstances change, but remains oriented toward Allah in
every state, holding fast to His door, acknowledging their need
for Him, and disclaiming any power or strength of their own.
In times of ease, the servant is grateful, seeing blessing as
coming from Allah and returning to Allah, meeting it with
praise and thanksgiving, translating their gratitude into
obedience, uprightness, and the good use of what they have
been given.
In times of hardship, the servant is patient, knowing that what
has befallen them could not have missed them, and that
behind every decree lies wisdom and mercy. Their heart
remains steady, they submit to their Lord’s command, and
they grow nearer [to Him], not further away.
In a state of sin, the servant repents, not persisting in
wrongdoing, nor too proud to return, but fleeing to Allah as a
broken soul in need flees, acknowledging their weakness,
hoping for His forgiveness.
In a state of obedience, the servant seeks forgiveness, claiming
no merit for themselves, not deceived by their own deeds, but
ever conscious of their shortcomings however hard they strive,
seeking forgiveness for the deficiency of their worship just as
they would for a sin. It is related, in the four collections of
Sunan, that the Prophet ﷺ used to seek his Lord’s forgiveness
three times immediately after concluding the prayer with the
closing salutation, saying:
“I seek Allah’s forgiveness”
i
(repeated
three times).
Such a servant turns wherever Allah’s command turns them,
their heart moving between gratitude and patience, their
tongue between praise and seeking forgiveness, their spirit
between fear and hope. This conscious movement between the
stations of servitude is the secret of remaining firm upon the
path, the root of safety from deviation, and the balance of
uprightness without excess or harshness.
Chapter 5: The Relationship Between Servitude and the
b
Stations of Faith
b
Servitude is not a station separate from the rest of the stations
of faith; rather, it is their root, from which they branch out,
their source, from which they draw nourishment, and their
centre, around which they are organized. Every sound station
of faith is, in truth, one of the fruits of sincere servitude, and
every disorder among the stations traces back to a defect in the
realization of servitude. This relationship can be shown as an
integrated, interlinked chain:
Sincere servitude → sincerity of intention (Ikhlas):
b
once
the meaning of servitude settles in the heart, one’s
purpose becomes devoted to Allah alone; nothing is
sought through one’s deeds but His pleasure, and nothing
is hoped for but His approval.
Sincerity → acceptance:
b
whatever is sincerely devoted to
Allah deserves to be raised up and accepted, for
acceptance is the fruit of purity of intention before it is the
fruit of an abundance of deeds.
Acceptance → tranquillity:
b
when the servant is certain
that their deed is accepted by Allah, their heart settles,
their turmoil vanishes, and they find rest in their Lord’s
mercy and favour.
Tranquillity → reliance upon Allah (tawakkul):
b
the
tranquil heart entrusts its affairs to Allah, depends upon
Him, and trusts in His good management.
Reliance → contentment:
b
whoever truly relies upon
Allah becomes content with whatever He decrees, for
their own choice has become subordinate to their Lord’s
choice.
Contentment → serenity (Sakinah):
b
when the servant is
content, a special stillness and an inner peace, unshaken
by storms, is poured into their heart.
Serenity → nearness to Allah:
b
serenity is the sign of
intimacy [with Allah], and nearness is the fruit of that
intimacy, and whoever draws near to Allah finds this
world and all that is in it to be of little consequence.
Thus, it becomes clear that the root is one, servitude, while the
fruits are many, the stations of faith, and that walking toward
Allah is not a leap between stations, but a gradual, natural
growth that begins with correcting one’s servitude and ends
with nearness to Allah, the Exalted.
This can be shown in a clear sequence: sincere servitude leads
to sincerity, sincerity leads to acceptance, acceptance leads to
tranquillity, tranquillity leads to reliance, reliance leads to
contentment, contentment leads to serenity, serenity leads to
nearness to Allah. The root, then, is one, while the fruits are
many.
Chapter 6: The Gravest Deviations from the Concept of
b
Servitude
b
Just as worship has a unifying root from which the stations of
faith branch out, it also has grave afflictions which, if they
creep into the heart, corrupt its true nature and divert the
course of one’s journey toward Allah, from a path of nearness
to a path of severance, while the one afflicted may imagine
themselves to be upon good, when in reality they are
regressing or going astray.
The gravest of these deviations do not always take the form of
open disbelief or manifest sin; they often come dressed in the
garb of religiosity, or in the name of freedom, or under the
banner of relying on one’s own deeds. For this reason,
exposing and explaining them is a necessity for anyone who
seeks true servitude:
Worship of the self:
b
following one’s own desire and
giving precedence to fleeting worldly wishes, making
one’s own inclination the supreme reference point, so
that worldly desires, immediate appetites, and
psychological leanings are given precedence over Allah’s
command and His law.
The standard, for such a person, becomes what I want, not
what pleases Allah; what I deem good, not what Allah has
commanded.
This form of deviation corrupts the very root of servitude, for
the true reality of servitude is to relinquish choice for oneself
and affirm that choice belongs to Allah.
Whoever worships their own desire is cut off from sincerity,
and stumbles along the path of the [spiritual] stations, for a
heart imprisoned by its own appetite cannot ascend the
degrees of nearness [to Allah].
Worship of created beings:
b
seeking people’s approval
at the expense of Allah’s approval, the heart turns
toward people’s gaze and their praise, so that one acts
for the sake of being praised, or abandons truth for fear
of being blamed, or changes one’s positions to preserve
one’s social image.
This deviation contradicts sincerity and turns the servant from
one oriented toward Allah into one attached to His creation.
Whoever attaches their heart to people is punished with
turmoil and anxiety, for the hearts of created beings are ever-
changing, and none of them possesses the power to benefit or
harm. There is no acceptance without sincerity, and no
sincerity alongside servitude to creation.
Worship of deeds:
b
relying upon acts of obedience
while forgetting the Bestower, the servant relies upon
their own deeds, sees merit in themselves on their
account, and forgets that success comes from Allah
alone, and that the favour belongs to Him alone. They
become deceived by the abundance of their prayer,
their fasting, their knowledge, or their da’wah, and the
