awareness of their own shortcoming and need weakens
in their heart. Allah says:
“Rather, Allah has conferred
i
favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you should
i
be truthful”
i
(Al-Hujurat 49:17), that is, it is Allah alone
who has conferred favour upon you by granting you
success in believing in Him, if you are truthful.
This deviation cuts off the path of nearness [to Allah], for one
does not draw near to Allah through bare deeds alone, but
through a sense of need and humility accompanying one’s
deeds.
Summary of the chapter:
b
these three deviations, worship of
the self, worship of created beings, and worship of one’s deeds,
share a single trait: each, in its own way, turns the heart away
from Allah.
Whoever is spared these deviations, and realizes pure
servitude, finds the doors of the [spiritual] stations opened to
them, and walks toward Allah upon a straight, secure path,
Allah willing.
Chapter 7: How Does the Muslim Train Themselves to
b
Realize Servitude?
b
Realizing servitude is not a claim to be raised, nor a wish to
be hoped for; it is continuous formation, constant struggle,
and a daily, conscious practice. For the heart wavers, the self-
weakens, and this world presses in, and the servant does not
remain firm upon the station of servitude except through a
clear, practical method by which they purify themselves and
correct their course. Among the most important features of
this method are the following:
Correcting one’s intention before every deed
b
, for
intention is the gateway to servitude, and by its soundness
the whole deed becomes sound. Before acting, the servant
asks themselves: why am I doing this? And for whom am
I doing it? If they find in their heart any turning toward
other than Allah, they struggle against it until their
purpose is Allah’s face alone. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ
said:
“Deeds are only by intentions.”
i
(Reported by Al-
Bukhari and Muslim.)
Abundant remembrance of Allah and seeking
b
forgiveness
b
, for remembrance is the life of hearts and
seeking forgiveness mends what is broken. Through both,
the heart is purified of heedlessness, the sense of servitude
is renewed, and the servant remains connected to their
Lord in every state. Allah says:
“…and the men who
i
remember Allah often and the women who remember [Him]…”
i
(Al-Ahzab 33:35).
Holding oneself to account daily
b
, the servant looks over
their day: what did they contribute, and where did they
fall short? They give thanks for their obedience, repent of
their disobedience, and resolve to reform, for without
such accounting, errors accumulate until they harden the
heart. Allah says:
“O you who have believed, fear Allah. And
i
let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow”
i
(Al-
Hashr 59:18). ’Umar ibn Al-Khattab (may Allah be
pleased with him) said:
“Hold yourselves to account before
i
you are held to account, for that will be easier for your reckoning,
i
or he said, lighter, and weigh yourselves before you are weighed,
i
and prepare for the greatest presentation: ‘That Day you will be
i
exhibited [for judgement]; not hidden among you is anything
i
concealed’”
i
[Al-Haqqah 69:18]. (
Az-Zuhd wa’r-Raqa’iq
i
, Ibn
Al-Mubarak.)
Contemplating the Noble Qur’an
b
, for the Qur’an is the
first book of servitude, containing Allah’s commands and
prohibitions, His promise and His warning, His names
and His attributes. Contemplating it acquaints the servant
with their Lord, and the more they come to know their
Lord, the more their servitude to Him deepens. Allah
says:
“[This is] a blessed Book which We have revealed to you,
i
[O Muhammad], that they might reflect upon its verses and that
i
those of understanding would be reminded”
i
Righteous companionship
b
, for the human being is weak
alone, but strong among their brothers and sisters.
Righteous companionship reminds one of Allah, assists
one toward obedience, calls one back from heedlessness,
and encourages one when weary. Allah says:
“O you who
i
have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true”
i
(At-
Tawbah 9:119), meaning, the believer should take care to
keep the company of people of truthfulness and
righteousness, for they help him toward good. He also
says:
“And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call
i
upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His
i
face”
i
(Al-Kahf 18:28), that is, keep to the company of
those who remember Allah and seek His pleasure. The
Prophet ﷺ said:
“A person follows the religion of his close
i
friend, so let each of you look closely at whom he befriends.”
i
(Reported by Abu Dawud and Al-Tirmidhi), meaning, a
person is influenced by their friend and their friend’s
character. Abu Dawud Al-Tayalisi related in his Musnad,
from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit, from Anas,
from Abu Musa, who said:
“The likeness of a righteous
i
companion is like that of a perfumer: if he does not give you any
i
of his perfume, you will still catch its scent from him; and the
i
likeness of a bad companion is like that of a blacksmith: if his
i
fire does not burn you, his smoke will still reach you.”
i
Constant supplication for the realization of servitude
b
for hearts are in Allah’s hand, and success comes only
from Him. The servant should frequently ask their Lord
to grant them sincere servitude, purity of purpose, and
firm steadfastness. Among the most comprehensive of
supplications is:
“O Allah, help me to remember You, to give
i
You thanks, and to worship You well.”
i
(Reported by Ibn Abi
Shaybah in
Al-Musannaf
i
Summary of the chapter:
b
whoever walks these paths
sincerely, progressing through them with patience, will find
their effect in their heart and conduct, and will move from
servitude in name to servitude in reality, from merely knowing
the path to walking it, Allah willing.
Chapter 8: The Fruit of This Part in the Muslim’s Life
b
When servitude is realized in the Muslim’s heart, in
knowledge, in state, and indeed, it no longer remains a mere
theoretical concept, but transforms into a living reality
reflected in their thought, their conduct, their choices, and
their outlook on themselves, this world, and the Hereafter.
The following are among the greatest fruits the Muslim reaps
from realizing this Part:
Clarity of purpose:
b
they know why they were created,
for whom they live, and where they are headed. Their
direction toward Allah becomes unified, confusion falls
away, and their course becomes upright.
Firmness upon the path:
b
they are not shaken by trials,
nor broken by obstacles, nor turned back by stumbling,
because their heart is bound to Allah, not to
circumstances.
Inner peace:
b
stillness in the heart, tranquillity in the soul,
and rest of conscience, because they are at peace with
their Lord, and whoever is at peace with Allah finds their
inward self at peace.
Balance between this world and the Hereafter:
b
they
take from this world only what they need and make the
Hereafter their goal, so they work, they strive, and they
cultivate the earth, without ever forgetting their final
destination.
Liberation from servitude to creation and desire:
b
they
are not enslaved by people’s opinions, nor led by appetite,
nor possessed by material things, but become master of
themselves, precisely because they are a servant of their
Lord.
The Muslim becomes a servant of Allah alone:
b
free from
everything else, self-sufficient through Allah rather than
dependent on others, honoured through obedience to
Him, and at peace through nearness to Him.
Summary of Part 1:
b
servitude is not a restraint that shackles a
person, but rather the greatest liberation; it is not a narrowing
of life, but the secret of its happiness. Whoever tastes the
sweetness of servitude to Allah will never again be satisfied
with any substitute.
Servitude is not merely one station among the stations of the
journey to Allah, it is the root from which every station
sprouts, and the foundation upon which the entire edifice of
faith is built. Whoever’s servitude is sound, their path is
sound; whoever’s path is upright, their life is upright;
whoever’s life is upright, their striving is accepted; and
whoever’s striving is accepted rises through the degrees of
nearness to Allah, the Exalted.
Servitude, then, is both the beginning and the end; it is both
the path and the destination. Whoever enters it sincerely
emerges from it with a living heart, a tranquil soul, and an
upright course.
Servitude to Allah, the Exalted, is the root upon which all the
[spiritual] stations are built, and it is the standard by which the
soundness of the path and the uprightness of conduct are
measured.
The more sincere and complete one’s servitude, the firmer and
more upright the [other] stations become; and every defect in
servitude is reflected as disorder in religion, disturbance in
understanding, deviation in conduct, and unease in life.
Part 2: The Muslim Belongs to Islam, as Identity and as
b
Method
b
This Part affirms that a Muslim’s belonging to Islam is not a
slogan to be raised aloft, nor a social inheritance one merely
settles for; it is a conscious identity, a comprehensive
commitment, and an integrated way of life embodied in belief
and conduct, in the Muslim’s relationship with themselves
and with others, and in their presence within society and
contemporary reality.
Its first chapter shows that Islam unites sound creed, which
reforms the heart; just legislation, which organizes life; and
elevated character, which purifies conduct, and that this
integration makes Islam fit to guide both the individual and
the building of society at once, without conflict between
worship and worldly development, nor between spirit and
matter.
Its second chapter highlights that true belonging is a
conscious, chosen belonging, springing from conviction,
understanding, and love, not a mere hereditary or formal
affiliation. Sincere belonging shows itself in obedience, in
uprightness, and in governing daily conduct by Islamic values,
as well as in bearing the responsibility of representing this
religion in word and deed.
Its third chapter establishes that Islam combines the fixity of
its fundamentals with the flexibility of its means: its fixed
principles are preserved and unchanging, while its variables
allow ample room for independent reasoning (ijtihad) and
renewal, in a manner that realizes the purposes of the Shari’ah
in every time and place. It also warns of the need for caution
regarding two deviant extremes:
1. The extreme of dissolution, which abandons Islamic
identity in the name of contemporaneity.
2. The extreme of extremism, which freezes upon a narrow
understanding and constricts what Allah has made
spacious.
The Part concludes that the truly belonging Muslim is one
who lives Islam as an identity in their heart, a method in their
thought, and conduct in their reality, remaining firm upon
their fundamentals, open to their age, balanced in their
understanding, and positive in their impact, thereby realizing
the meaning of belonging that pleases Allah, benefits the
human being, and builds up life. It contains five chapters.
Chapter 1: Islam Is Creed, Law, and Character
b
This chapter establishes a central truth: that Islam is not a
collection of rituals detached from life, nor a dry system of
laws, nor a set of abstract moral exhortations, but an
integrated structure whose pillars are a creed that sets faith
right, a law (Shari’ah) that organizes action, and a character
that purifies conduct. If any of these pillars is disturbed, the
balance in the Muslim’s personality, and in the image of Islam
in reality, is disturbed along with it.
Creed
b
is the foundation upon which the Muslim’s
personality is built, for it acquaints them with their Lord,
with the purpose of their existence, and with their
destiny, instilling in their heart monotheism, certainty,
dependence on Allah, awe of Him, and hope in His
mercy. The more deeply rooted the creed in the heart, the
firmer a person’s steadfastness against temptation, and
the more upright their conduct in private and in public,
for righteous conduct is the fruit of living faith, not mere
outward compliance.
The Shari’ah
b
is the practical application of that creed
within the reality of life, organizing a person’s
relationship with their Lord through acts of worship, their
relationship with people through transactions, and their
relationship with themselves through what preserves
their religion, mind, self, wealth, and honour. The
Shari’ah is not a restriction of freedom, but a direction for
it; not a heavy burden upon the human being, but a mercy
and a justice that secure their interests in this world and
the next.
Character
b
is the spirit that runs through both creed and
law together, making faith living and effective, and
legislation beautiful and beloved. The Muslim’s honesty,
trustworthiness, justice, forbearance, mercy, and
humility are not secondary matters, but lie at the very
heart of the religion, by them is the truth of one’s
religiosity measured, and the sincerity of one’s belonging
to Islam recognized.
This chapter shows that separating these three dimensions is a
grave error: there is no sound creed without a behavioural
effect, no applied law without character, and no firmly rooted
character without a doctrinal foundation. Islam, in its
complete form, is a faith confirmed by action, an action
purified by character, and a character springing from a heart
united in devotion to Allah.
Thus, the balanced Muslim personality is formed: a heart
bound to Allah, conduct disciplined by His law, and dealings
with others founded upon noble character, becoming a living
model of Islam, a silent call to it before ever being words or
speech.
Chapter 2: The Comprehensiveness of Islam for the
b
Individual and Society
b
This chapter establishes that Islam did not come to reform a
single aspect of human life to the exclusion of others but
brought a comprehensive method that addresses the human
being in themselves, sets right their relationship with their
Lord, organizes their relationship with people, and lays the
foundations for building a righteous, cohesive society. Islam
addresses the individual to reform them into an upright
human being and addresses the community to establish
through it a nation that bears witness to humanity.
On the individual’s side, Islam attends to forming the human
being from within before the without instilling faith in their
heart, purifying their soul of the diseases of arrogance, envy,
and ostentation, accustoming them to Allah’s watchfulness in
secret and in the open, and refining their conduct through acts
of worship that purify the spirit, rulings that discipline the
limbs, and character that elevates the self. The individual in
Islam is not a mere number within society, but an essential
building block, and their own soundness is a necessary
precondition for the soundness of the community.
On society’s side, Islam establishes an integrated system of
values and structures that safeguard rights, realize justice and
mutual solidarity, prevent oppression and aggression, and
build people’s relationships upon mercy, honesty, and
trustworthiness, organizing the affairs of the family, the
economy, the judiciary, politics, and social relations upon a
foundation of justice and responsibility, not upon desire and
narrow self-interest.
This chapter affirms that the relationship between the
individual and society in Islam is one of integration, not
conflict: the righteous individual contributes to building a
righteous society, and the righteous society helps the
individual toward uprightness. The individual’s right is not
lost in the name of the collective, nor is the collective’s interest
neglected in the name of individual freedom, rather, the
balance is achieved that preserves human dignity while
safeguarding the unity of the nation.
The chapter further shows that Islam’s comprehensiveness
does not mean rigidity, but rather the capacity of the Islamic
method to absorb changing reality and direct it according to
fixed purposes, such that Islam remains present in every time
and place, fit to reform souls and to build civilizations.
The chapter concludes that Islam, when correctly understood
and applied, is a comprehensive project of reform: it builds the
individual in faith and conduct, establishes society in justice
and mutual mercy, and produces a nation that carries the
message of guidance for the whole of humanity.
Chapter 3: The Difference Between True Belonging and
b
Hereditary Belonging
b
This chapter addresses a pivotal issue in the reality of the
[Muslim] nation: distinguishing between belonging to Islam
as a conscious choice and sincere commitment and belonging
to it as a mere hereditary or social affiliation that does not go
beyond the name or the outward form. Not everyone born a
Muslim is necessarily a true believer in the full sense of
belonging, just as the truth of belonging is not measured by
slogans, but by awareness, conduct, and commitment.
True belonging springs from firm faith and inner conviction;
the one who possesses it grasps the meaning of Islam and the
purpose of their existence and embraces its commands and
prohibitions out of love and reverence, not out of mere
imitation or conformity to their surroundings. This kind of
belonging bears fruit in obedience, uprightness, eagerness to
learn, and a sense of responsibility toward the religion and the
propagation of its values.
Hereditary belonging, by contrast, is when a person is
affiliated with Islam by virtue of their birth, environment, or
customs, without this being accompanied by any true
understanding of its meanings or serious commitment to its
rulings. Religion becomes, for such a person, more a cultural
identity than a way of life, and they may content themselves
with appearances and rites, while the effects of faith remain
absent from their conduct and character.
This chapter shows that the danger of hereditary belonging lies
in the fact that it produces a fragile religiosity, quickly swayed
by doubts, weak in the face of temptations, because its roots
were never planted in the heart upon a foundation of
knowledge and certainty. True belonging, by contrast,
produces a firm character, confident in its religion, capable of
distinguishing truth from falsehood, and equipped to carry the
message of Islam within a changing reality.
The chapter also explains that the transition from hereditary
to true belonging is possible and available to every Muslim,
through seeking knowledge, contemplating the Qur’an,
holding oneself to account, keeping the company of the
righteous, and connecting acts of worship to their purposes
and meanings, until Islam becomes a daily, renewed choice,
not merely a historical inheritance.
The chapter concludes that a Muslim’s worth in Allah’s sight
is not based on themselves or their environment, but on the
sincerity of their faith and God-consciousness, and that the
nation cannot rise except through those who belong to Islam
in awareness, love, and commitment, not merely in name and
outward form.
Chapter 4: Manifestations of Behavioural Belonging
b
If true belonging to Islam rests upon awareness and
conviction, its practical field is conduct, for the sincerity of
belonging is not known by frequent claims, but by what
appears in one’s limbs as commitment, in one’s character as
uprightness, and in one’s dealings as honesty and
trustworthiness. Conduct is the daily translation of the
Muslim’s identity and method.
Among the most prominent manifestations of behavioural
belonging is adherence to religious duties and obligations:
praying on time, taking care with ritual purity, giving alms,
fasting Ramadan, and observing the other rites of Islam are
not merely inherited customs, but a practical expression of
submission to Allah and reverence for His commands. This
belonging grows firmer through attentiveness to the
recommended acts and forms of obedience, not out of
formality, but out of love and a desire for nearness to Allah.
Another manifestation is governing one’s character by Islamic
values: the Muslim is truthful in speech, fulfils trusts, is just in
judgement, forbearing when angered, merciful to the weak,
and does good to all people. Character is not an external
adornment, but a clear sign of the depth of one’s belonging to
the religion.
Behavioural belonging also appears in the mastery of one’s
appetites and commitment to the boundaries of Shari’ah: the
Muslim chooses the lawful even when it is harder, and avoids
the unlawful even when it is tempting, out of the awareness
that Allah’s pleasure takes precedence over the desire of the
self.
This belonging is also evident in commitment to Islamic
identity without blind zealotry or dissolution: the Muslim
appears confident in their values, preserving their
distinctiveness, open toward others with justice and kindness,
without compromising their fixed principles.
Among its important manifestations, too, is a positive
presence within society: the belonging Muslim does not live in
isolation, but contributes to reform, offers wise counsel,
participates in serving people, works to spread good, and
stands with truth wherever it may be found.
This chapter concludes that behavioural belonging is the
practical measure of the sincerity of one’s inward belonging,
for the more a Muslim’s worship is committed, their conduct
upright, and their dealings sound, the more this demonstrates
the firmness of their belonging to Islam as an identity and a
way of life.
Chapter 5: Belonging Between Fixity and Renewal
b
This chapter addresses a delicate equation in the Muslim’s life:
how to remain fixed in belonging regarding fundamentals and
identity, while remaining renewable in means, understanding,
and application, without an excess that freezes, or a laxity that
dilutes:
The meaning of belonging in this conception:
b
belonging
in Islam is not merely a slogan or a cultural identity, but
rather: a doctrinal bond with Allah, the Exalted; a
methodological commitment to what has come in the
Noble Qur’an and the Sunnah; and a sense of
responsibility toward religion, the nation, and humanity.
Whoever belongs to Islam draws honour from their
religion, derives from it their vision of the universe, life,
and humanity, and makes their supreme reference point
revelation, not desire, nor external pressure.
Fixity in belonging, what does not change?
b
Fixity
means holding fast to the definitive fundamentals that
admit no alteration, foremost among them: the fixity of
creed, monotheism, faith in Allah, His angels, His books,
His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree; the
fixity of the great values, honesty, trustworthiness,
justice, mercy, chastity, and excellence; and the fixity of
the ethical framework, that the lawful remains lawful and
the unlawful remains unlawful, however times may
change.
Renewal in belonging, what does change?
b
Renewal
does not mean changing the religion, but rather reviving
its meanings within hearts, applying it well to changing
reality, and developing means and methods. The fields of
renewal include renewal of understanding, connecting
texts to their great underlying purposes and
understanding them considering reality; renewal of
discourse, using language closer to people, clearer in
meaning, gentler in style; and renewal of means, using
media, technology, and modern education in service of
da’wah. Renewal, then, is a movement in means and
understanding, not in fundamentals and principles.
The relationship between fixity and renewal:
b
the two
are not opposites, but two wings, fixity protects against
deviation, and renewal protects against rigidity. A defect
in either produces harm: fixity without renewal leads to
rigidity, harshness, and disconnection from reality;
renewal without fixity leads to the dilution and loss of
identity.
Features of balanced belonging:
b
sound belonging is
characterized by pride without zealotry, openness
without dissolution, commitment without extremism,
and mercy without vagueness [that is, without speech
becoming unclear or incomprehensible].
The effects of balanced belonging in a Muslim’s life:
b
inner tranquillity and psychological stability, clarity of
positions and choices, the ability to engage positively
with one’s age, and a sense of responsibility toward
reform.
Summary:
b
true belonging is fixity in fundamentals and
renewal in understanding and means, and through this the
Muslim remains true to their identity, present in their age,
influential in their reality, and a witness before people through
their religion and character.
Section One: The Fixed Principles of Islam and the
b
Variables of the Age
b
This section establishes the great rule for understanding Islam
and for how the Muslim engages with reality: that this religion
combines firmly rooted, unchanging fundamentals with vast
space for independent reasoning (ijtihad) and renewal that
engages with the variables of time and place. Through this
balance, the religion is preserved from distortion while
retaining its constant capacity to keep pace with life.
The fixed principles of Islam are the definitive fundamentals
that admit no alteration or compromise, encompassing the
great doctrines, the pillars of Islam, the fundamental ethical
values, the general principles of the Shari’ah, and its supreme
purposes, such as the preservation of religion, life, intellect,
lineage, and property. These fixed principles represent the
identity and essence of Islam, and their remaining constant is
the secret of the religion’s continued fitness for every time and
place.
The variables of the age, on the other hand, fall within the
sphere of means, methods, and the practical application of
rulings, matters open to independent reasoning according to
recognized benefit and changing circumstances, such as
modes of education, means of da’wah, methods of
administration, the organization of state and society, modern
technologies, and the like. These variables are not understood
in isolation from the fixed principles but are governed and
directed within their framework. This section shows that error
occurs at one of two extremes:
1. An extreme that glorifies the variables and treats them as
though they were fixed principles, thereby narrowing
what is broad and making things difficult for people.
2. An extreme that dilutes the fixed principles and subjects
them to desires and pressures, thereby emptying religion
of its content.
The correct approach is precise discrimination between what
is a fixed foundation and what is a changeable branch,
followed by positive engagement with the age through sound
understanding and insight, preserving the purity of Islam’s
identity while, at the same time, enabling it to direct reality
and shape the future.
Section Two: Confronting Dissolution and Extremism
b
This section addresses one of the gravest challenges facing
religious belonging in the modern age: deviation between two
opposing extremes, the extreme of dissolution and laxity, and
the extreme of extremism and excess, both of which take the
Muslim outside the middle path (wasatiyyah) that Islam
brought.
Dissolution into the “other” means the Muslim’s loss of their
doctrinal, cultural, and behavioural distinctiveness, until they
become a follower in their thought, values, and lifestyle,
imitating others without discernment, and growing shy of
displaying their own identity. This may reach the point of
doubting the fixed principles of their religion or belittling them
in the name of progress and contemporaneity, a path that
ultimately leads to spiritual emptiness, psychological
disturbance, and severance from one’s roots.
Conversely, extremism and excess mean transgressing the
bounds of moderation, being overly rigid in understanding
and application, narrowing what Allah has made broad, and
obligating people to things the Shari’ah never obligated them
to, accompanied by harshness in discourse, poor treatment of
others, and an exclusionary view of them. This path harms the
image of Islam, drives people away from it, and turns
religiosity from a mercy and a guidance into a burden and a
source of aversion.
This section shows that the correct Islamic approach is the
way of moderation and balance (wasatiyyah), founded upon
a balanced understanding of the texts, combining ultimate
purposes with specific rulings, and distinguishing between the
fixed and the variable, the definitive and the probabilistic, and
between what is intended for its own sake and what is merely
a means to it. It also explains that confronting these two
deviations comes through: establishing methodical religious
knowledge rather than superficial culture; developing
awareness of the overarching purposes of Islamic law; raising
Muslims to understand the proper handling of disagreement
and to have breadth of heart; and connecting religiosity to
character, mercy, and good conduct.
This section concludes that sound religious belonging is a
conscious, balanced belonging, fixed in its fundamentals,
flexible in its means, which preserves the Muslim’s identity
from dissolution, and protects them from sliding into
extremism, so that Islam remains, in their life, a light of
guidance, a method of construction, and a message of mercy
to all the worlds.
Summary of Part 2: The Muslim Belongs to Islam, as
b
Identity and as Method
b
This Part affirms that belonging to Islam is not a mere nominal
or hereditary affiliation, nor a fleeting emotional state, but a
conscious choice, a firmly rooted identity, and a
comprehensive way of life embodied in belief, thought,
conduct, and action.
The Part has shown that Islam is an integrated religion,
uniting the creed that sets the heart right, the law that
organizes life, and the character that purifies conduct, and that
this integration is the foundation for forming the balanced
Muslim personality, capable of both firmness and giving.
It has also clarified that true belonging differs fundamentally
from formal or hereditary belonging: the former rests upon
understanding, conviction, love, and commitment, while the
latter is content with a name and an appearance, without any
deep effect on conduct and choices. Hence, practical conduct
and daily character are the true measure of the sincerity of
one’s belonging.
The Part has likewise shown that Islam unites the fixity of its
fundamentals with the flexibility of its means: its fixed
principles are preserved and unchanging, and its variables
offer broad scope for independent reasoning and renewal,
enabling the Muslim to engage positively with their age
without compromising their identity.
It has also warned of the danger of deviating between the two
extremes of dissolution and extremism, affirming that the safe
path is moderation and balance, founded upon knowledge,
sound understanding, attention to the underlying purposes,
and good character.
The Part concludes that the truly belonging Muslim is one
who lives Islam as an identity in their heart, a method in their
thought, and conduct in their reality, remaining firm upon
their religion, open to their age, positive in their society, and
a witness before people through their character before their
words, and through their deeds before their slogans.
Belonging to Islam is a conscious commitment to its method,
not a mere slogan, and it is a natural fruit of sincere servitude.
Part 3: The Muslim Emulates the Messenger ﷺ
b
This Part establishes a great principle of faith: that emulating
the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is not a secondary matter or an
optional practice, but a genuine pillar in realizing sincere
servitude to Allah, and a clear sign of the sincerity of one’s
love and belonging to this religion. The Prophet ﷺ is the one
who conveyed Allah’s message, who explained His law, and
who provided the complete practical model for embodying
Islam in the reality of life.
This Part shows that emulating the Messenger ﷺ encompasses
every aspect of life: creed, worship, character, transactions,
social and foreign relations, managing disagreement, facing
trials, and building the individual, the family, and society. He
is the excellent example (uswah hasanah) in whom the
meanings of mercy, justice, wisdom, patience, humility,
courage, and good character are embodied.
The Part also clarifies that true emulation does not mean
[merely copying] outward appearances or confining oneself to
externals, but rather a comprehensive understanding of the
Prophet’s ﷺ guidance that unites the purposes of his Sunnah
with its specific rulings, and its spirit with its applications,
while accounting for the differences of time and place in
matters of means, alongside the fixity of values and
fundamentals.
The Part further affirms that love for the Prophet ﷺ is
measured by the extent of one’s obedience to him, one’s
reverence for his Sunnah, one’s propagation of his guidance,
one’s defence of him, and one’s walking upon his path in
da’wah and reform, not by mere sentiment or claim.
The Part concludes that the more a Muslim emulates the
Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the closer they draw to Allah, the more
upright their life becomes, the more blessing enters their work,
and the more they are accepted among people, for the Prophet
ﷺ is the practical path to realizing Islam in its most beautiful
and complete form. It contains three chapters.
Chapter 1: The Meaning and Reality of Emulation
b
Emulating the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is among the greatest
expressions of servitude to Allah, and among the clearest
proofs of the sincerity of one’s faith and love, for true
following of Allah is realized only through following His
Messenger, and Allah’s commands and prohibitions cannot
be understood in their full practical sense except through the
guidance and Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.
Emulation, in its true reality, means that the Muslim makes
the Prophet ﷺ their model and example in belief, worship,
character, conduct, and choices, walking upon his path with
knowledge and insight, not blind imitation or mere emotional
admiration.
This chapter shows that true emulation rests upon three
fundamental pillars:
Knowledge of the Prophet’s ﷺ guidance
b
, for there is no
emulation without knowledge. One must learn his
biography, his Sunnah, and his noble characteristics, and
understand his purposes, so that one’s following is based
on awareness and understanding, not mere conjecture or
ignorance.
Sincere love for him ﷺ
b
, for love is the inner motive for
emulation. The greater a servant’s love for their Prophet
ﷺ, the easier it becomes for them to follow him, hold fast
to his Sunnah, and give precedence to his guidance over
their own desires and people’s customs.
3. This chapter also clarifies that emulation is not confined
to one aspect to the exclusion of others, but is
comprehensive of everything authentically established
from the Prophet ﷺ, whether in speech, action, or tacit
approval, while distinguishing between what constitutes
general legislation for the whole nation, what pertained
specifically to him, and what belongs to the category of
custom and means, in which variation is permissible.
This chapter concludes that the true meaning of emulation is
that the Prophet ﷺ transforms, in the Muslim’s life, from a
revered historical figure in the mind into a living model
present in conduct, decision, and direction, thereby realizing
the meaning of following that yields Allah’s pleasure, the
soundness of the heart, and the uprightness of life. It contains
two sections:
Section One: The Difference Between Love and Following
b
Distinguishing between love and following is among the
important issues in the matter of emulating the Messenger of
Allah ﷺ, for many people imagine that mere heartfelt love
suffices to realize emulation, whereas the Qur’anic and
Prophetic method establishes that sincere love is never
separate from following, and that following is the practical
proof of the sincerity of that love.
Love is the heart’s inclination toward the Prophet ﷺ, its
reverence and honouring of him, its joy in mentioning him, its
yearning for his Sunnah, and its defence of him. This love is a
great foundation of faith, a servant’s faith is not sound without
it, and it is a heart-state that stirs the emotions and prompts
reverence and veneration.
Following, however, is the translation of that love into
practical reality, through obeying his commands, avoiding
what he prohibited, emulating his guidance in worship,
transactions, and character, and referring to his Sunnah in
matters of dispute. It is manifest, practical conduct, indicating
what lies within the heart of love and reverence.
This section shows that love without following is an
incomplete claim, it may be accompanied by emotion, but it
lacks practical evidence, while following without love is dry
and burdensome, lacking spirit and sweetness. Perfection lies
in uniting the two: love in the heart and following in action.
It also shows that the measure of the sincerity of one’s love is
the extent to which one’s daily life conforms to the guidance
of the Prophet ﷺ, in worship, character, dealings, and choices,
the more one holds to his Sunnah, the more this proves the
sincerity of one’s love.
This section concludes that the correct path in emulation is for
love to become commitment, and for commitment to become
a firmly rooted habit, so that the Muslim lives with the
Prophet ﷺ, with love in their heart, following in their conduct,
and his guidance present in their reality.
Section Two: Following in Acts of Worship and
b
Transactions
b
This section affirms that emulating the Messenger of Allah ﷺ
is not complete unless its effect appears in two great
dimensions of a Muslim’s life: the dimension of worship,
which binds them to their Lord, and the dimension of
transactions, which organizes their relationships with people.
Following is not restricted to devotional rites alone, nor to
general character alone, but is a comprehensive method
directing the Muslim’s entire life.
In worship, following is realized through performing what the
Prophet ﷺ legislated in the manner he explained, without
innovative addition or deficient omission.
The Muslim takes care to learn the manner of prayer as the
Prophet ﷺ prayed it, the form of ablution as he performed it,
and the rulings of fasting, pilgrimage, and almsgiving as he
legislated them, bearing in mind that acceptance with Allah
depends upon sincerity and conformity together. Through
this, following in worship becomes an expression of the
perfection of servitude, and a sincere submission to Allah’s
command.
In transactions, following is manifest in adherence to the
Prophet’s ﷺ guidance regarding honesty, trustworthiness,
justice, fulfilling covenants, good neighbourliness, mercy
toward the weak, fairness in disputes, and avoiding fraud,
betrayal, and injustice.
The Muslim who truly emulates the Prophet ﷺ does not
separate their religiosity in the mosque from their religiosity in
the marketplace, at work, or at home, but makes the Sunnah
of the Prophet ﷺ the standard for their conduct in every place.
This section shows that following in worship preserves the
purity and soundness of religion, while following in
transactions preserves its beauty and its effect in reality, and
through both together, the complete image of Islam as Allah,
Mighty and Sublime, intended it, becomes manifest.
It also shows that among the signs of sincere following is the
Muslim’s keenness to correct their worship, review their
conduct, hold themselves to account for shortcomings, and
constantly strive to draw nearer to the guidance of the Prophet
ﷺ.
This section concludes that true following means the Muslim
lives with the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ as a firm method in
their worship, and a just standard in their transactions, thereby
realizing the perfection of emulation, the beauty of religiosity,
and soundness of state in this world and the next.
Chapter 2: The Comprehensiveness of Prophetic Emulation
b
This chapter establishes that emulating the Messenger of
Allah ﷺ is not confined to a particular aspect of life, nor to a
narrow circle of behaviours, but is a comprehensive emulation
extending to thought, heart, and action, encompassing the
affairs of the individual, the family, and society.
The Prophet ﷺ was not merely a preacher in speech, but a
complete practical model for embodying Islam in reality.
The comprehensiveness of emulation means that the Muslim
makes the Prophet ﷺ the supreme reference point in building
their character, following his example in his profound faith in
Allah, his reliance upon Him, his awe of Him, and his hope in
His mercy, as well as in his honesty, trustworthiness, patience,
forbearance, humility, courage, and good treatment of people
regardless of their circumstances.
Emulation likewise extends to the spheres of family and social
life: the Muslim follows the Prophet’s ﷺ example as a merciful
spouse, a compassionate father, a wise educator, a good
neighbour, and a loyal companion, making their home a
practical field for applying the Sunnah, not merely a place to
live.
The comprehensiveness of emulation also extends to the
sphere of da’wah and reform: the Muslim learns from the
Prophet ﷺ wisdom in discourse, gentleness with those being
called, patience with harm, gradualism in bringing about
change, and a concern for guiding people rather than for
personal victory.
This chapter shows that comprehensive emulation does not
mean replicating every outward form and detail, but
emulating the purposes, the spirit, and the meanings, while
adhering to the fixed rulings and considering the differences
of time and place with respect to means and methods.
The chapter concludes that the comprehensiveness of
Prophetic emulation means that the Muslim lives with the
Messenger of Allah ﷺ as a living example present in their
thought, a leader guiding their method, and a supreme model
for their conduct, so that Islam becomes, in their life, a moving
reality, not merely theoretical knowledge or historical
admiration. It contains two sections:
Section One: The Prophet ﷺ as Educator, Leader, and
b
Spouse
b
The Prophet ﷺ was a teacher and an educator, an imam and a
leader, the head of a town and a head of state, a husband and
a father. This section shows that the comprehensiveness of
Prophetic emulation is clearly manifest in the multiplicity and
integration of the Prophet’s ﷺ roles, for he was a complete
model of the Muslim human being across different positions
and responsibilities, such that every Muslim, whatever their
position in life, can find in the Prophet’s biography a model
suited to their own reality.
The Prophet ﷺ was a teacher who conveyed Allah’s message
with clear explanation, brought meanings closer to people,
addressed both minds and hearts, and employed wisdom,
parables, and gradualism in teaching.
The Prophet ﷺ was an educator who attended to purifying
souls before multiplying information, instilling faith,
strengthening character, gently correcting errors, encouraging
good, and being patient with shortcomings.
He ﷺ was, in the people’s daily affairs, like the head of a town:
judging between them, resolving their disputes, checking on
their circumstances, attending to the poor and the weak, and
sharing in their joys and sorrows. He was likewise a head of
state, establishing justice, concluding treaties, organizing
internal and external relations, and founding a society built
upon both law and mercy together.
And in his home, the Prophet ﷺ was a merciful husband,
treating his family kindly, being gentle with them, valuing
their feelings, and sharing in household affairs, and a
compassionate father, raising his children upon faith and
character, instilling values in them through example before
words.
This section concludes that the greatness of the Prophet ﷺ lies
not merely in his being the bearer of a message, but in his being
a practical model in every position of his life, and that
comprehensive emulation of him requires the Muslim to
follow his example in whatever role they occupy, whatever
their position or responsibility, so that Islam becomes a living
reality embodied in their daily life.
Section Two: Emulation in Character Before Appearances
b
This section affirms that the essence of emulating the
Messenger of Allah ﷺ rests first upon emulating his character
and his practical example, before attending to appearances
and formalities, for character is the spirit of the Sunnah, the
greatest thing that distinguished the Prophet’s ﷺ personality,
and the clearest thing that drew hearts to his message.
The Prophet ﷺ was the highest example in honesty,
trustworthiness, mercy, forbearance, forgiveness, humility,
justice, patience, and good treatment of others, and this
character was the silent call that preceded much of his speech
and words.
For this reason, the truly emulating Muslim is one who strives
for these values to be reflected in their daily conduct with their
family, neighbours, colleagues, and those who agree or
disagree with them.
This section shows that preoccupation with appearances
alone, without attention to the essence of character, may lead
to a distorted image of religiosity, in which rites appear
without their effect appearing in conduct, whereas the
Prophetic method closely links worship with good character,
and makes the perfection of character part of the perfection of
faith, as the Prophet ﷺ said:
“The most complete of the believers in
i
faith are those best in character.”
i
(Reported by Ibn Wahb in his
book
Al-Jami’
i
It also shows that emulating character does not mean
neglecting legitimate outward practices but rather giving
precedence to inward formation over outward formation, so
that outward appearances become a natural fruit of sincere
character, not a mask concealing a defect in conduct.
This section concludes that whoever seeks true emulation of
the Prophet ﷺ should make their first measure: have I grown
more truthful? More merciful? Humbler, forbearing, and just?
If these meanings are realized, this is evidence that one is
walking the path of correct emulation, making the Sunnah of
the Prophet ﷺ a living reality walking upon the earth, through
his character before his appearances.
Chapter 3: The Danger of Separating the Sunnah from
b
Reality
b
This chapter addresses a serious problem in understanding
and applying religion: treating the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ as
a heritage preserved in books, or texts for blessing and reading,
without its ever becoming a living method guiding reality. The
Sunnah was not transmitted merely to be memorized, but to
be lived in conduct, translated into decisions, and drawn upon
in building the individual and society.
Separating the Sunnah from reality practically means
disabling its essential function, so that knowledge of it
becomes abstract, theoretical knowledge, producing no real
effect on character, transactions, or ways of life. This
separation empties emulation of its content and turns
religiosity into a formal image devoid of spirit. This chapter
shows that among the gravest consequences of separating the
Sunnah from reality are:
The weakening effect of religion on conduct
b
, where acts
of worship are performed, but are not reflected in
honesty, trustworthiness, and justice, so that a
contradiction appears between what a person worships
with and what they live in their daily dealings.
The distortion of Islam’s image
b
, because people do not
judge religion through abstract texts, but through the
conduct of its followers; when the Sunnah is absent from
reality, the beauty of Islam disappears.
Opening the door to desires and deviant
b
interpretations
b
, for when the Sunnah is isolated from
directing life, it becomes easy to replace it with human
ideas or foreign standards given precedence over the
guidance of the Prophet ﷺ.
The chapter also shows that the Sunnah came to address the
real, practical issues of human life: within the family, the
marketplace, the factory, the workshop, social relations, the
management of disagreement, and the building of values, for
it is a way of life before it is a collection of legal texts.
The chapter affirms that the correct path is to connect the
Sunnah to reality with conscious understanding, through
grasping its purposes, recalling its wisdom, and applying it to
new developments with sound understanding and insight, so
that it remains present in the Muslim’s life, guiding rather than
absent, and effective rather than marginalized (that is, not
neglected or set aside without application; ethical values ought
never to be marginalized in society, nor should they be
neglected).
The chapter concludes that the nation’s remaining upon the
right path depends on the extent to which the Sunnah of the
Prophet ﷺ is present in its reality, and that the greatest form of
emulation is that the Sunnah transforms from pages that are
merely read into a life that is actually lived, from information
stored away into ever-renewed conduct that shapes the human
being and builds up society. It contains two sections:
Section One: Turning the Sunnah into Frozen Ritual
b
This section shows that among the gravest forms of separating
the Sunnah from reality is reducing it to formal practices or
limited rituals performed at particular times, without their
becoming a comprehensive method that guides conduct and
shapes character, for the Sunnah, in its fundamentals, came to
build the human being from within and without, not to
become empty gestures devoid of meaning.
Turning the Sunnah into frozen ritual means focusing on
outward performance while neglecting its purposes and aims.
Some people maintain certain outward practices of the
Sunnah while their effect fails to appear in honesty,
trustworthiness, mercy, justice, guarding one’s tongue, or
good conduct, thereby severing worship from character, and
emptying the Sunnah of its spirit. This section shows that this
course leads to several negative effects, the most important of
which are:
Formal religiosity without spirit
b
, where performance
abounds while effect diminishes, weakening the influence
of religion on the self and on life.
Weariness with worship
b
, for worship, when emptied of
meaning, turns into a heavy habit rather than a beloved
act of nearness [to Allah].
Misunderstanding of the Sunnah
b
, some people imagine
the Sunnah to be mere formal details, whereas its true
reality is that it is a comprehensive way of life.
This section also shows that the remedy lies in reviving the
meanings and purposes behind the acts of the Sunnah,
connecting every act of worship to its educational aim, and
every Prophetic guidance to its behavioural effect, so that the
Sunnah returns to its original function: the formation of the
righteous human being.
This section concludes that the Sunnah is not meant to be
frozen ritual, but living guidance that purifies the heart, sets
conduct right, and builds a society founded upon values, and
through this, true emulation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is
realized.
Section Two: Understanding the Sunnah Within Its
b
Purposive Context
b
This section affirms that among the greatest means of
connecting the Sunnah to reality, and freeing it from rigidity
or misunderstanding, is viewing it within its purposive
context, that is, understanding it in light of the great aims it
came to achieve, and the wisdoms the Lawgiver intended by
legislating it, rather than confining oneself to the outward
wording or forms detached from their meanings.
The Prophetic Sunnah did not come as scattered, unconnected
rulings, but within an integrated system aiming to preserve
religion, build the human being, realize justice, spread mercy,
purify souls, and establish balance in life, and every hadith or
Prophetic guidance falls, ultimately, under one of these great
purposes.
This section shows that understanding the Sunnah within its
purposive context prevents falling into two dangerous
extremes:
The extreme of rigidity
b
, which is content with outward
appearance, applying texts without regard to their
underlying reasons, wisdoms, and outcomes.
The extreme of laxity
b
, which invokes purposes as a
pretext to disable or bypass the texts.
The correct method is to unite text and purpose: the text is
respected and followed, and the purpose is understood and
kept in mind, thereby realizing conscious, balanced following.
This section also shows that bearing the purposes in mind
assists in applying the Sunnah to new and emerging matters,
making it fit to address contemporary issues without
compromising its fixed principles or departing from its spirit.
This section concludes that understanding the Sunnah within
its purposive context transforms it from rigid texts into a
living, ever-renewed method, and makes emulation of the
Prophet ﷺ a conscious, insightful emulation that realizes the
purposes of the Shari’ah and produces a balanced human
being and a rightly guided society.
Summary of Part 3
b
Emulating the Messenger ﷺ is the practical formation of
servitude and belonging, without which religion becomes
merely theoretical. This Part affirms that emulating the
Messenger of Allah ﷺ is not a mere supplementary aspect of
the Muslim’s life, but the practical path to establishing
servitude to Allah and embodying true belonging to Islam, for
the Prophet ﷺ is the complete applied model of what Allah
wants from His servants in belief, conduct, and method.
The Part has shown that the meaning of emulation rests upon
knowledge of the Messenger’s ﷺ guidance, sincere love for
him, and practical obedience to his commands, and that
uniting these pillars is what produces true following. It has
also clarified that emulation encompasses both worship and
transactions together, for there is no religiosity without sound
worship, and no sincere worship without an ethical and
behavioural effect.
The Part has highlighted the comprehensiveness of Prophetic
emulation across every sphere of life, the Prophet ﷺ being a
model for the teacher and the educator, the leader and the
ruler, the husband and the father, the individual in solitude,
and society in its relations, making his biography a source of
guidance for every Muslim, whatever their position or
responsibility.
The Part has also warned of the danger of separating the
Sunnah from reality, whether by turning it into frozen ritual
or by removing it from its purposive context, affirming that the
Sunnah came to be lived and applied, not merely preserved
theoretically.
The Part concludes that emulating the Messenger ﷺ is the
practical formation that carries servitude from the level of
feeling to the level of conduct, and belonging from the level of
claim to the level of commitment, the closer a Muslim draws
to the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ, the closer they draw to
Allah, the more sincere their belonging to their religion, and
the greater their effect upon themselves and their society.
Part 4: The Muslim as a Seeker of Knowledge and One
b
Who Is Raised by an Educator, the Sheikh as a Model
b
This Part establishes a great meaning in building the Muslim
character: that the Muslim, on their journey with Allah, is
always a seeker of knowledge, never content with what they
have attained, never stopping at a fixed limit, for knowledge
is the path of guidance, the foundation of uprightness, and the
standard by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. It
also shows that the presence of a mentoring sheikh in the life
of the seeker of knowledge represents a practical model of
purification and guidance, uniting knowledge with action, and
understanding with formation.
Seeking knowledge in Islam is not an intellectual luxury, nor
is it confined to a particular group, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim”
i
(Agreed
upon), rather, it is an obligation according to one’s
circumstance, and a necessity for building sound faith,
correcting worship, disciplining conduct, and properly
applying religion to reality. The more knowledge a Muslim
gain, the more their awe of Allah grows. Allah says:
“Only
i
those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge”
i
(Fatir 35:28), and their insight broadens, and their capacity to
face doubts and desires strengthens.
This Part shows that the mentoring sheikh is not merely a
transmitter of information, but an educational model,
teaching with their tongue and educating with their state
before their words, assisting the seeker of knowledge to purify
their soul, hold their heart to account, order their priorities,
and walk the path of uprightness with steadiness and balance.
The Part also clarifies that the relationship between the seeker
of knowledge and the sheikh should be founded upon respect,
trust, and conscious reception, while preserving the standing
of knowledge and its people, without excess regarding
individuals or the deification of human beings, for the true
standard is the Book and the Sunnah, and the sheikh is a guide
to the path, not a substitute for the guide [i.e., not a substitute
for revelation itself].
The Part concludes that combining the pursuit of knowledge
with formation at the hands of a mentoring sheikh produces a
conscious Muslim, firmly grounded in their understanding,
upright in their conduct, capable of worshipping Allah with
insight, and of serving their religion and nation with sincerity
and wisdom. It contains three chapters.
Chapter 1: Knowledge and Purification Without
b
Deification
b
This chapter establishes that among the greatest purposes of
seeking knowledge in Islam is the attainment of guidance and
the purification of the soul, not the manufacture of human
idols, nor the attachment of hearts to individuals. Knowledge,
in its true reality, is a means to know Allah, to revere Him, to
comply with His command, and to walk toward Him with
insight, and purification (tazkiyah) is the fruit of this
knowledge when it transforms into awe, uprightness,
character, and righteous conduct.
Islam always links knowledge with action and understanding
with purification, the goal is not an abundance of information,
nor expansive argumentation, but knowledge that produces
awe, leads to obedience, purifies the heart of its diseases, and
refines the soul of its inclinations.
At the same time, this chapter warns against the deviation of
deifying individuals, however elevated their scholarly or
da’wah standing, for infallibility belongs to none but the
prophets, upon them be Allah’s prayers and peace, and human
beings err and are correct in turn. The scholar, the sheikh, and
the educator are to be revered and respected, and knowledge
is taken from them, but they are not to be made the standard
of truth, rather, their words are to be measured against the
Book and the Sunnah. This chapter shows that the correct
approach rests upon three foundations:
Revering knowledge, not individuals
b
, for true standing
belongs to the truth that is conveyed, not to the one who
conveys it.
Benefiting from scholars while preserving the balance
b
we take from them, thank them, and pray for them, while
recognizing that they are human beings who err and are
correct in turn.
Making purification a constant purpose
b
, such that the
effect of knowledge is manifest in character, humility,
and good treatment of others, not in arrogance and
superiority.
This chapter concludes that the conscious Muslim combines
receiving knowledge from people of learning with freeing their
heart from attachment to individuals, so that their loyalty is to
the truth, their reference point is the Book and the Sunnah,
and their constant effort is directed toward purifying
themselves. Through this, they attain beneficial knowledge,
sound formation, and uprightness free of excess or deviation.
Chapter 2: The Standing of the Sheikh and the Scholar in
b
Islam
b
This chapter shows that God-fearing scholars hold an exalted
standing in Islam, for they are the bearers of revelation, the
heirs of the prophets, and guides upon the path to Allah,
through them religion is preserved from distortion, the
Shari’ah is safeguarded from ignorance and desire, and people
are guided in their worship and their dealings.
The scholar, in the Islamic method, is not merely a religiously
educated person, but one who bears a mission, combining
knowledge with action, and carrying out the functions of
explanation and teaching, da’wah and guidance, and
purification and formation. The nearer a scholar draws to
Allah, and the more sincere they are in their work, the greater
their effect upon souls, and the more enduring their impact
upon the nation.
This chapter affirms that revering and respecting scholars is an
act of worship through which one draws near to Allah,
involving as it does the veneration of Allah’s symbols, the
preservation of the dignity of knowledge, and encouragement
to seek it, yet this reverence does not mean infallibility, does
not excuse error, and does not permit following them without
insight.
The chapter also shows that the mentoring sheikh represents
a special category of scholar, for in addition to teaching, they
attend to purifying souls and correcting conduct, taking their
students by the hand along the path of uprightness, and
helping them to struggle against their own selves, order their
priorities, and achieve balance between knowledge and
action.
This chapter shows that the nation owes scholars: love, prayer
on their behalf, the propagation of their knowledge, defence
of them, and benefiting from them; and that scholars, in turn,
owe the nation: sincerity, honesty, humility, gentleness with
learners, and connecting people to Allah rather than to
themselves.
The chapter concludes that the standing of the sheikh and the
scholars in Islam is one of reverence and appreciation, not
veneration, deification, or worship, and that the rightly-guided
Muslim is one who combines respect for the people of
knowledge with holding fast to the standards of Shari’ah,
making their loyalty to the truth, their guide the Book and the
Sunnah, and their relationship with scholars one of benefit
and guidance, not blind zealotry and following. It contains
two sections:
Section One: Scholars Are the Heirs of the Prophets
b
This section affirms that the greatest honour scholars have
attained in Islam is that Allah has made them heirs of the
prophets, not in wealth or status, but in the greatest of
inheritances: the inheritance of knowledge and guidance. The
prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, came to bring
people out of darkness into light. Allah says to His Prophet:
“[This is] a Book which We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad],
i
that you might bring mankind out of darknesses into the light, by
i
permission of their Lord, to the path of the Exalted in Might, the
i
Praiseworthy”
i
(Ibrahim 14:1). Scholars, after them, carry out
the same task: preserving revelation, explaining its meanings,
teaching people their religion, and guiding them to Allah’s
path.
The scholars’ inheritance from the prophets means that they
carry the mission of explanation and conveyance, carry out
the function of reform and guidance, and strive to spread the
truth, confront falsehood, and correct deviation, each
according to their knowledge, capacity, and sphere.
This section shows that this inheritance is a responsibility
before it is an honour, placing upon scholars’ shoulders a
tremendous duty embodied in sincerity, honesty, scholarly
integrity, distance from personal desire, connecting people to
Allah rather than to themselves, and acting upon what they
know before calling others to it.
It also shows that a scholar’s rank is not measured by the
number of their followers, their fame, or their position, but by
the extent of their adherence to the Book and the Sunnah, their
awe of Allah, their benefit to people, and the effect of their
knowledge in purifying souls and reforming reality.
This section concludes that Muslims’ awareness of the
meaning of scholars’ inheritance from the prophets instils in
them love and reverence for scholars and eagerness to learn
from them, while also instilling in scholars a constant sense of
responsibility and self-watchfulness, so that they may
discharge this great trust in the manner that pleases Allah, the
Exalted.
Section Two: The Function of Teaching and Purification
b
This section shows that the mission of scholars and the
mentoring sheikh in Islam is not confined to transmitting
information or explaining rulings alone, but rests upon two
inseparable, complementary functions: teaching and
purification, for through teaching, truth is known, and
through purification, truth is lived.
The function of teaching consists in explaining sound creed,
elucidating the rulings of the Shari’ah, clarifying what is
lawful and unlawful, interpreting the texts of the Book and the
Sunnah, and training students of knowledge in methodical
understanding and sound reasoning, so that their knowledge
is founded upon evidence, not blind imitation or personal
desire.
The function of purification, meanwhile, is concerned with
the hearts and souls of learners, raising them upon sincerity,
awe of Allah, God-consciousness, good intention, struggle
against the self, adornment with virtuous character, and
freedom from arrogance, ostentation, self-admiration, and
other diseases of the heart. Knowledge unaccompanied by
purification may turn into an argument against its possessor,
or a means for disputation and self-exaltation on earth.
This section shows that combining teaching and purification
is the Prophetic method for building the human being, and
that neglecting either dimension produces a defect in
character: knowledge without purification breeds harshness,
arrogance, and aridity; purification without knowledge may
open the door to deviation, innovation, and misguidance.
It also shows that the successful mentoring sheikh is one who
balances these two dimensions, teaching their students
beneficial knowledge, raising them to act upon it, and being
an example to them in their conduct before their speech.
This section concludes that the function of teaching and
purification is at the heart of the educational process in Islam,
and through it a God-fearing seeker of knowledge is formed,
combining sound understanding, a sound heart, and upright
conduct, thereby being of benefit to themselves and their
nation.
Chapter 3: Governing Principles for the Relationship with
b
the Religious Sheikh
b
This chapter addresses the foundations and governing
principles that should underlie the relationship between the
seeker of knowledge and the religious sheikh, so that it
remains a relationship of formation, benefit, and guidance,
not one of blind following, nor one of conflict and
estrangement. The soundness of this relationship is among the
greatest sources of blessing in knowledge and soundness in
one’s educational path:
The first of these principles
b
is sincerity and good intention,
the student should intend, in seeking knowledge, Allah’s face,
the reform of their own self, and acting upon what they learn,
not fame, argument, or self-vindication.
The second
b
is respect and reverence, the student reveres their
sheikh, preserves their standing, and maintains good manners
with them in word and deed, for this is part of revering
knowledge, not the veneration of individuals for their own
sake.
The third
b
is verifying the method, that the sheikh be known
for holding fast to the Book and the Sunnah, for sound creed,
and for good conduct, since formation is not sound except
upon a sound method.
The fourth
b
is the Shari’ah standard, the student should know
that their sheikh’s words are to be taken or rejected [according
to the Shari’ah], and that infallibility belongs to none but the
prophets, so they weigh what they hear against the Book and
the Sunnah, while preserving courtesy and respect.
The fifth
b
is sincerity in counsel, if the student sees a clear
error, they offer counsel with courtesy and wisdom, without
exposure or offence, seeking Allah’s pleasure and preserving
the sanctity of knowledge.
The sixth
b
is balanced independence, the student should not
dissolve into the sheikh’s personality to the point of losing
their own capacity for thought and discernment, nor should
they dispense with the sheikh out of arrogance but should
walk a balanced course between the two.
This chapter concludes that the correct relationship between
student and sheikh is one of learning and purification, respect
and awareness, benefit without deification, and through this
the blessing of knowledge is realized, and the student’s course
upon the path of Allah remains upright. It contains four
sections, followed by the summary.
Section One: Obedience in What Is Right, Not in Sin
b
This section establishes a great principle governing the
relationship between the seeker of knowledge and the sheikh,
indeed, between any Muslim and anyone from whom they
receive guidance, namely, that obedience is due only in what
is right, and never in sin or in violation of the Shari’ah. The
unchanging fundamental is that absolute obedience belongs to
Allah, the Exalted, and to His Messenger ﷺ; obedience to
anyone else is conditioned upon truth.
If the sheikh or educator commands something that conforms
to the Book and the Sunnah, and realizes a legitimate benefit,
the student must obey them in that, think well of them, and
benefit from their guidance and experience. But if they
command something sinful, or call to an innovation, or
contradict an explicit text or an established principle of the
Shari’ah, it is not permissible for the student to obey them,
rather, it is their duty to refrain with courtesy, and to explain
the truth with wisdom. The Prophet ﷺ said:
“Obedience is only
i
in what is right (ma’ruf).”
i
(Reported by Al-Bukhari.)
This section shows that understanding this principle protects
the student from blind following, just as it protects the sheikh
from being placed in a position befitting none but Allah and
His Messenger, and at the same time, it preserves scholars’
standing, for obedience in what is right is itself a form of
reverence and benefit.
It also shows that refraining from obedience in sin does not
constitute disrespect, nor does it diminish the sheikh’s
standing; rather, it is commitment to Allah’s law, while
respect, appreciation, and good manner of address remain.
This section concludes that the rightly-guided student is one
who combines hearing and obeying in what is right, with
refraining from wrong with courtesy and wisdom, thereby
preserving their religion, safeguarding their heart, and keeping
their relationship with the sheikh one of guidance and benefit,
not one of deification or conflict.
Section Two: The Danger of Inflating the Sheikh’s Standing
b
This section addresses one of the dangerous deviations that
may afflict the course of formation and the pursuit of
knowledge: inflating the standing of the sheikh, raising him
above his legitimate rank, until he becomes, in the eyes of
some students, not an educator, counsellor, and guide upon
the path, but an infallible figure or an absolute reference,
beyond review or discussion.
This section affirms that Islam has exalted the standing of
God-fearing scholars, and commanded their reverence and
respect, while at the same time denying infallibility to anyone
but the prophets, upon them be Allah’s prayers and peace.
Every scholar’s word may be taken or rejected; they err and
are correct in turn; and their speech is judged against the Book
and the Sunnah, not the reverse. This section shows that
inflating the sheikh’s standing leads to many corruptions, the
gravest of which are: disabling human reason and disciplined
critical thinking; justifying errors under the pretext of thinking
well [of the sheikh] or his elevated station; transforming the
educational relationship into one of psychological and
spiritual dependency; and opening the door to religious
exploitation in the name of formation and purification.
Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
“Everyone’s
i
words may be taken or rejected, except the occupant of this grave”

Jami’ Bayan Al-’Ilm wa Fadlih

book

i

Al-Risalah
