This section also shows that this inflation harms not only the
student, but the sheikh as well, for it may push him, without
his even realizing it, toward self-admiration or domineering,
and distance him from the spirit of humility that is the
hallmark of sincere scholars.
This section establishes that the correct approach rests upon
balance: revering the sheikh and benefiting from his
knowledge and experience, while recognizing his human
nature and its limits, and binding one’s heart to Allah, the
Exalted, first, and to the truth second, not to individuals.
This section closes by affirming that sound formation is that
which produces students who are free through the truth,
connected to Allah, following the evidence, loving their
scholars, without deifying them or making them the standard
of truth and falsehood.
Section Three: Giving Precedence to the Sheikh Over the
b
Text
b
Giving precedence to the sheikh, scholar, or educator over the
texts of revelation is among the gravest manifestations of
deviation in understanding the relationship between student
and sheikh, for it transforms the standard from revelation
being the judge over individuals, into individuals being the
judge over revelation, a complete inversion of the method
Islam brought.
This section establishes that the true fundamental in Allah’s
religion is that the Book and the Sunnah are the supreme
reference point, and that the words of anyone after the
Messenger of Allah ﷺ are to be measured against the evidence,
accepted if they conform to it, and rejected if they contradict
it, however elevated that person’s standing may be. It shows
that manifestations of giving precedence to the sheikh over the
text include: interpreting texts or disabling them to conform
with the sheikh’s or scholar’s opinion; justifying error by
claiming the sheikh’s special status or esoteric knowledge;
excusing the sheikh’s or educator’s errors as though they were
genuinely correct; rejecting evidence when it contradicts what
the student has grown accustomed to from their sheikh; and
considering disagreement with the sheikh a departure from the
method or a betrayal of the path.
This section also shows that this approach leads to the
deification of individuals, opens the door to innovations and
deviations, and strips the texts of their authority in directing
hearts and conduct. It affirms that the correct method
combines love and reverence for the sheikh; sincere recourse
to the text; reliance upon the understanding of trustworthy
scholars; and readiness to return to the truth whenever it
becomes clear.
This section closes by affirming that the greatest honour for
the sheikh himself is to be a follower of the text, not one
followed instead of it, to guide his students to Allah and His
Messenger, not to himself, for through this, formation is
sound, the method is upright, and the nation remains bound
to revelation, not to individuals.
Section Four: Disabling the Mind in the Name of Formation
b
This section addresses a dangerous phenomenon that
sometimes occurs in certain educational environments:
disabling the mind and suspending thought in the name of
formation and purification, on the pretext that excessive
questioning or the exercise of reason contradicts good
manners, weakens submission, or corrupts the heart.
This section affirms that Islam did not come to abolish the
intellect, but to liberate it, refine it, and guide it, making it a
tool for understanding revelation, contemplating Allah’s
signs, and distinguishing truth from falsehood. For this
reason, the Qur’an is filled with commands to reflect, reason,
and observe. Allah says:
“Then let mankind look at his food”
i
(Abasa 80:24), and:
“Then let man look at what he was created
i
from”
i
(At-Tariq 86:5), and:
“Do they not look at the camels, how
i
they are created? And at the sky, how it is raised? And at the
i
mountains, how they are erected? And at the earth, how it is spread
i
out?”
i
(Al-Ghashiyah 88:17–20), and:
“[This is] a blessed Book
i
which We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], that they might
i
reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding would be
i
reminded”
i
(Sad 38:29), and:
“Then do they not reflect upon the
i
Qur’an, or are there locks upon [their] hearts?”
i
(Muhammad
This section shows that sound formation is not built by killing
questions, nor by subjecting minds to the sheikh’s will, but by
building an aware intellect and a living heart, in which
understanding is joined with awe, and knowledge with action.
Among the manifestations of disabling the mind in the name
of formation are: preventing the student from asking or
discussing under the pretext of good manners with the sheikh;
treating any independent thought or criticism as objection to
the sheikh or ill intent; being content with rote instruction
without explaining the Shari’ah evidence and wisdom behind
it; and tying guidance to the extent of one’s surrender to the
sheikh rather than to the extent of one’s following of the truth.
This section warns that this course produces followers rather
than students of knowledge, and creates personalities weak
before doubts, quick to submit, and lacking in insight.
This section establishes that the balanced method is one that
raises the student upon: respecting scholars, asking well-
formed questions, exercising reason considering revelation,
and submitting to the text after understanding it to the best of
one’s ability.
It closes by affirming that the greatest purpose of formation is
to produce a human being free through truth, aware of their
religion, firm upon their method, neither an unthinking
follower, nor an uninformed objector.
Summary of Part 4
b
The sheikh is a means to guidance, not an end in himself, and
whoever exceeds this boundary with him corrupts their own
religion without realizing it. This Part has shown that Islam
made knowledge and purification a path for building the God-
fearing human being and connected this path to God-fearing
scholars as guides upon the way, not deities to be worshipped,
nor infallible figures to be followed unconditionally. The
sheikh, in the Islamic method, is a means to guidance,
pointing to Allah and His Messenger and assisting in
understanding and applying religion, not an end to which
hearts become attached.
This Part has affirmed that scholars and sheikhs hold an
exalted standing, for they are the heirs of the prophets, and
their function is teaching and purification, yet this standing is
governed by Shari’ah principles that prevent excess and
deification, and that preserve the balance between reverence
and disciplined criticism, and between obedience in what is
right and refraining from what is sinful.
This Part has also highlighted the danger of deviation in the
relationship with the sheikh, whether through inflating his
standing, giving him precedence over the text, or disabling the
mind in the name of formation, for this leads to corrupting the
method, and transforms formation from the building of a
human being free through truth into the manufacture of
unthinking followers. The Part concludes that sound
formation is that which: binds hearts to Allah, Glorified and
Exalted, first; makes revelation the supreme standard; reveres
God-fearing scholars without deifying them; and builds an
aware intellect and a reverent heart.
Whoever makes the sheikh an end in himself goes astray, and
whoever makes him a guide to Allah is rightly guided, and
through this, the course of the seeker of knowledge becomes
upright, and their formation bears fruit in firm faith, beneficial
knowledge, and righteous deed.
Complete Summary of the Book
b
This book proceeds from a central truth: that the balanced life
of the Muslim is not built upon a single dimension, nor made
upright through one station to the exclusion of another, but
rests upon four great, interconnected stations, each reinforcing
the others, together forming the personality of the God-fearing
Muslim who unites purity of creed, soundness of method,
correct emulation, and sound formation. The balanced life of
the Muslim rests upon four interconnected stations:
A servant of Allah, the Exalted, an unrivalled
b
foundation.
b
Servitude is the root from which all other
stations spring; it is the reality of human existence and the
purpose of one’s creation. The Muslim is a servant of
Allah alone, their heart bound to Him, their submission
to Him, their hope in Him, their fear of Him, and any
station that loses its connection to servitude turns from
worship into mere habit, and from nearness into an
empty form devoid of spirit. When servitude settles in the
heart, the human being is liberated from attachment to
creation, and their outlook toward this world and the
Hereafter is set right.
One who belongs to Islam, an identity and a method.
b
Belonging to Islam is not a slogan to be raised, nor a
name inherited, but an awareness of identity, a
commitment to method, and a practical translation of
creed into conduct, a belonging that combines fixity upon
the fundamentals of the religion with awareness of the
variables of the age, preserving the Muslim’s authenticity
without insularity, and granting them the capacity for
engagement without dissolution. Through this, Islam
becomes, for them, a way of life, not merely a cultural
framework [that is, not merely a part of culture or social
custom, but something deeper and more essential, a
framework being something that surrounds and
organizes a thing].
One who emulates the Messenger, upon him be prayers
b
and peace, a practical model.
b
Emulating the Messenger
ﷺ is the practical bridge that carries the Muslim from the
realm of theory to the realm of application. The Sunnah
is not frozen ritual, nor mere formal appearance, but a
comprehensive method in worship, character,
transactions, and the building of family and society. True
emulation begins from within before the without, from
character before appearances, so that the Muslim
becomes an image of Prophetic guidance in their reality.
A seeker of knowledge at the hands of a sheikh, a
b
means of formation.
b
Islam made the pursuit of
knowledge a path to guidance, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Whomever Allah wishes well for, He grants him understanding
i
of the religion”
i
(Agreed upon), and connected this path to
God-fearing scholars, but on a foundation of balance:
reverence without deification, obedience in what is right,
and constant recourse to the Book and the Sunnah. The
sheikh is a means to guidance, not an end in himself; his
role is to point to Allah and His Messenger, and to assist
in purifying the self and building sound understanding,
not to be made the standard of truth and falsehood. Any
imbalance between these stations, undisciplined
precedence given to one over another, produces disorder
in understanding and conduct.
Comprehensive Summary
b
When these four stations are realized in a Muslim’s life in their
correct form, a balanced character is formed: a heart bound to
Allah, an identity rooted in Islam, a model found in the
Messenger, and a path found in knowledge and purification.
Through this, the Muslim lives their Islam as servitude, as
belonging, as emulation, and as learning, becoming upright as
an individual, reforming their family, contributing to building
their nation, and realizing the purpose for which they were
created: the worship of Allah, the Exalted, and the cultivation
of the earth according to His method.
Conclusion of the Book
b
This ordering is not a mere mental theorization, but a way of
life, and reforming the condition of the [Muslim] nation
begins with reforming the balance of the individual, when they
come to know whom, they worship, to which religion they
belong, whom they emulate, and from whom they learn. We
close with a supplication that Allah grant the reader balanced
understanding, sincere action, and firmness upon the path,
and we ask Allah to send prayers and peace upon His servant
and Messenger, Muhammad ibn Abdullah, and upon his
family and companions, and upon all who follow them in
righteousness until the Day of Judgement. Our final call is that
all praise is due to Allah, Lord of all the worlds.
